- Dependency/compatibility decision: an initial Rust standard sort panicked on the full mixed sequence (83523), because Python object comparison (notably tuple-contained NaNs) is not a total order. It cannot be safely handed to Rust's total-order sorting API. Added the private `object_argsort.rs` adapter following the comparison/partition order of NumPy 2.4.0's [npy_aquicksort_impl](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.0/numpy/_core/src/npysort/quicksort.cpp) and [npy_aheapsort](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.0/numpy/_core/src/npysort/heapsort.cpp). This is a compatibility-specific adapter, not a replacement general-purpose sort library; Arrow sort does not define Python heterogeneous-object comparison or these observable non-total ties. Tuple rank vectors still use standard Rust sorting because their order is total. No dependencies added. Preserved upstream attribution/BSD-3-Clause in `crates/core/NUMPY-LICENSE.txt`, reflected combined licensing in core's Cargo metadata, and verified package listing includes the notice and adapted source. Future replacement must preserve this pinned behavior while supporting fallible/non-total comparisons.

### Bool/float object chaining and block contract (2026-09-19)

- Previous goal turn made verified production progress. Current source inspection traced Pandas `_is_uniform_join_units`, `_concatenate_join_units`, `JoinUnit.get_reindexed_values` and `concat_compat`. Bool/float behavior is asymmetric: bool-first goes through generic concatenation, numerically converts bool values and then boxes floats as object; a non-all-NA float-first block can retain its floating dtype through the uniform fast path. The fast-path decision is group-wide, not per-column. These are actual installed-source semantics, not a proposed symmetric promotion table.

### Numeric dataframe promotion: source contract frozen, implementation pending (2026-09-19)

This continuation established a necessary compatibility constraint before extending `joined_type`: actual Pandas 2.3.3 results cannot be derived from the two Arrow column dtypes alone. Equal logical frames with identical float64 columns/values produce different appended dtypes depending on whether the all-NaN column shares a Pandas block with a non-NaN column. A consolidated `[x=NaN,y=2]` plus float32 rows yields `[float64,float64]`; separate left blocks yield `[float32,float64]`. Input values/dtypes are identical; the block partition differs. ### Object-array price arithmetic stages (2026-09-19)

- Added `object_price_advantage`, `ObjectPriceArithmetic` and concrete `FloatObjectArithmetic`. The generic boundary accepts independent input/quotient/difference/output/error types, completes all division callbacks before subtraction and all subtraction callbacks before multiplication, propagates the first failure, and retains the exact output object for singleton results. Completed-stage temporaries are released before the next stage. Nonzero-dimensional object results retain NaN and infinities; zero-dimensional input uses the scalar-finalization hook, including numeric cleanup or a custom missing-`.size` error. Zero baseline returns an object-result variant containing integer zeros with original shape and skips direction/callbacks.
- Real NumPy characterization exposed an important distinction: zero-dimensional object input becomes a Python scalar after division, whereas a shape-[1] object array remains an object array until final `.item()`. The custom Item fixture therefore fails with `'Item' object has no attribute 'size'` only for zero-dimensional input; the native adapter preserves the same callback sequence and failure stage. The concrete float adapter implements both paths without a Python runtime.
- Initial absolute-stride sorting failed the broadcast trace by producing repeated adjacent items instead of C-order rows. Implemented NumPy's zero-stride-aware stable axis ordering, retaining negative-stride logical direction and ignoring ambiguous broadcast/singleton strides. The narrow compatibility ordering follows the [official iterator construction source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy/v2.4.0/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/nditer_constr.c); ndarray's generic `map` explicitly permits arbitrary visitation order, so it cannot provide this observable callback contract. Existing ndarray/std/thiserror suffice; no dependency or lockfile changes in this slice.
- The unchanged upstream `price_advantage` AST runs with real NumPy in `tests/fixtures/object_price_advantage.py`. Another 768 float-object cases compare exact finite/signed-zero bits, NaN classification, infinities, scalar/array distinction, zero baselines and invalid directions. ### Configured live SAOE loader and adapter factory (2026-09-17)

- Added `SaoeBacktestDataLoader::load_shared` and `ConfiguredLiveSaoeAdapterFactory`. The loader retains the original shared order, releases every order guard before market callbacks, and observes the source callback boundaries in order: initial cache key, quote timestamps, post-quote interval/deal fields, deal price, then a fresh post-deal stock read for volume. The factory then reads live frequency, captures position, resolves the original decision's start step, loads the already-eager baseline prices and publishes the concrete live numerical adapter. It implements the existing live registry factory trait, so no parallel registry or numerical engine was introduced.
- `LiveSaoeAdapterRuntime` provides the narrow post-loading runtime boundary. `SharedExecutionCalendar` implements it directly, including fixed-minute conversion, month rejection, overflow handling, original live-decision range resolution and calendar poisoning. ## Runtime constants

- Contract: Preserve `REG_CN`, `REG_US`, `REG_TW`, `EPS`, `INF`, `ONE_DAY`, `ONE_MIN`, and `EPS_T` values and stable lowercase region representations.
- In scope: Runtime constants; typed `Region` parsing, display, iteration, and Serde representation; live Python differential test.
- Out of scope: `float_or_ndarray`, which is a Python-only constrained `TypeVar` used by two RL order-execution annotations. Its Python contract is captured now; the Rust numeric abstraction belongs with the future RL array representation.
- Compatibility decisions: Use signed `chrono::TimeDelta` to match Pandas Timedelta semantics. Keep exact public string constants alongside a typed enum. Region parsing is intentionally lowercase and case-sensitive, matching the existing values.
- Dependencies: `chrono` with only `std` for time deltas; `serde` for stable configuration/wire representation; `strum` for generated enum display, parsing, string access, and variant inventory; `serde_json` only for tests. These replace custom general-purpose implementations.
- Verification commands (from `D:\code\github\qlib-rs`):
  - `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
  - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
  - `cargo test --workspace --all-features`
  - `cargo tree --workspace --duplicates`
  - `cargo llvm-cov --workspace --all-features --fail-under-lines 100 --fail-under-file-lines 100 --fail-under-functions 100 --fail-under-regions 100 --show-missing-lines`
  - `cargo +nightly llvm-cov --workspace --all-features --branch --show-missing-lines`
- Results: Formatting and strict Clippy pass. Three Rust tests pass, including a live differential import of the original Python module. The only duplicate major dependency is `syn` 2/3 through third-party `strum_macros` and `serde_derive`; no project crate directly depends on either version. An attempted run of upstream `tests/misc/test_utils.py` stopped during collection because the local Python environment lacks `setuptools_scm`; that broad consumer test is not a constants contract test, so no heavy Qlib environment was installed. The focused live differential test imports `constant.py` directly and verifies every runtime value plus the deferred TypeVar metadata.
- Coverage: `constants.rs` has 6/6 regions, 1/1 functions, and 6/6 executable lines covered (100% each). Nightly branch instrumentation reports 0 missed of 0 instrumentable branches; the `match` arms are represented as covered regions rather than LLVM branch counters. HTML report: `target/llvm-cov/html/index.html`.
- Known gaps: `float_or_ndarray` is deferred as described above.
- Next candidate: Qlib configuration region defaults; completed in the next section.

## Region defaults

- Contract: Preserve the exact CN/US/TW `trade_unit`, nullable `limit_threshold`, and `deal_price` values applied by `QlibConfig.set_region`.
- In scope: Owned typed `RegionConfig`; exhaustive `Region::defaults` mapping; Serde JSON round trips; source-level Python differential test.
- Out of scope: The rest of the mutable global `QlibConfig`, mode templates, path resolution, logging setup, Redis fallback, and component registration.
- Compatibility decisions: Return an owned config so callers cannot mutate shared defaults as they could with an exposed global map. Keep `deal_price` as `String`, because later Qlib configuration accepts expression strings and tuple forms outside these simple defaults. Keep exact binary `f64` thresholds.
- Dependencies: Reuse workspace `serde` derives and `serde_json` test support. No additional dependency or custom configuration parser is needed for this typed leaf contract.
- Verification commands (from `D:\code\github\qlib-rs`):

## Frequency value object

- Contract: Preserve all supported month/mon, week/w, day/d, and minute/min aliases; case-insensitive parsing; zero counts; normalized display/debug strings; approximate minute deltas; nearest resampling-source selection; and Pandas-compatible fixed Timedelta unit behavior.
- In scope: `FrequencyUnit`, `Frequency`, parsing errors, normalized Serde string representation, approximate delta arithmetic, nearest compatible source selection, and fixed `TimeDelta` conversion.
- Out of scope: Calendar generation, market-session indexing, DataPathManager filesystem selection, and actual time-series resampling.
- Compatibility decisions: Counts use `num_bigint::BigUint`, preserving Python's arbitrary-precision non-negative `int` contract, including `0min` and values beyond `u64::MAX`. Fixed `TimeDelta` conversion accepts a signed `BigInt` and reports an explicit range error only when Chrono cannot represent the requested duration. Preserve the upstream month approximation exactly as `30 * 7` days even though it appears unusual. Return `Option<Frequency>` from nearest-source selection instead of Python's accidental string-or-object union while preserving ordering and normalized result text.

## Feature-frequency fallback

- Contract: Preserve the exact requested-frequency first attempt; defer parsing until that attempt fails with `ValueError`/`KeyError`; preserve exact request spelling on direct success; retry month/week/day at `day` and then `1min`; retry minute at `1min`; repeat `day` when the original request is already `day`; propagate all non-retryable and final-attempt failures; and return the frequency that actually produced the data.
- In scope: An object-safe, `Send + Sync` `FeatureProvider` boundary; owned query and resolved-result DTOs; Arrow `RecordBatch` batches; Python-sized disk-cache policy; typed retryable/non-retryable errors; exact request cloning across fallbacks; and a live Python mock-provider differential.
- Out of scope: Concrete local/remote storage providers, generalized Qlib market/filter instrument specifications, asynchronous I/O, Python bindings, dynamic library discovery/loading, plugin ABI version negotiation, and dataframe benchmark aggregation.
- Compatibility decisions: Provider results remain ordered `Vec<RecordBatch>` values and are returned unchanged. `FeatureQuery` uses explicit symbol and field vectors for the only current caller (`backtest.report`); a future adapter must encode Qlib's broader market/dict/filter instrument forms before claiming full `D.features` input parity. Invalid frequency strings are deliberately accepted when a provider accepts them directly, because upstream parses only after a retryable failure. `FeatureProviderError::Value` and `Key` mirror the only caught Python exceptions; `Other` is terminal.
- Plugin boundary: The Rust trait is dependency injection and compile-time plugin readiness, not a stable native ABI. Local, remote, test, or future plugin adapters can implement it without changing fallback logic. A dynamic plugin layer must later wrap the Arrow schema/batch contract using `abi_stable`, Arrow FFI/IPC, or Wasmtime components after isolation and deployment requirements are known; raw Rust trait-object dylibs are intentionally not promised as ABI-stable.
- Dependencies: Reuse Apache Arrow 59.2.0 for columnar interchange, `chrono` for typed time bounds, `num-bigint` for Python-sized cache policy integers, and `thiserror` for classified public errors. No new crate is required. `inventory`/`linkme`, `abi_stable`, and Wasmtime were not added because this slice defines provider semantics but does not yet require discovery, native loading, or sandbox execution.

## Time-series index selection

- Contract: Preserve Qlib's lazy stable index sort, both supported two-level index orders, inclusive exact timestamp slicing, reversed-range `None`, empty/index-only `None`, duplicate source order, and `NaT` sorting/filter behavior for the `method=None` stage of `resam_ts_data`.
- In scope: Explicit Arrow index columns; single datetime and instrument/datetime layouts; Arrow second/millisecond/microsecond/nanosecond timestamp units; timezone metadata; optional typed bounds; stable sorting with an original-row ordinal; an O(n) already-sorted fast path; and live execution of the original Python functions extracted by AST.
- Out of scope: Built-in/callable aggregation, Pandas partial-date strings such as `"2024-01"`, Python binding conversion, and timezone-string parsing. These are later aggregation or adapter slices; this slice does not claim full `resam_ts_data` parity.
- Compatibility decisions: Arrow index columns remain explicit in the returned `RecordBatch`. Exact typed bounds use Pandas' signed nanosecond range. Unbounded null timestamps sort last and remain; either bound excludes them. The public operation returns typed layout/type/range errors. Arrow sort/take/filter calls operate only on equal-length columns, generated in-bounds indices, and same-batch masks; those dependency invariants are documented assertions rather than impossible public error variants.
- Plugin boundary: Selection is deterministic dataframe plumbing and is not pluginized. The following aggregation slice is the extension point: built-in methods should use third-party Arrow kernels, while custom aggregators should sit behind a narrow object-safe trait or a versioned Wasmtime/FFI boundary after isolation requirements are known.
- Dependencies: Added Apache Arrow `arrow-ord` 59.2.0 for comparators and stable lexicographic indices, and `arrow-select` 59.2.0 for `take` and filter kernels. Both match the existing Arrow 59.2.0 columnar stack and Rust 1.85 MSRV. Polars 0.55.2 was evaluated but not selected for this stage because it introduces a separate Arrow implementation and no advantage over the matching Arrow kernels; it can be reconsidered when aggregation benchmarks justify it.

## Time-series built-in aggregation

- Contract: After the existing stable selection stage, preserve Pandas' default-kwargs `all`, `sum`, `mean`, `prod`, and grouped `first`/`last` behavior; group two-level inputs by non-null instrument in sorted key order; skip null/NaN values; preserve empty-reduction identities; apply per-column dtype rules; drop null instrument groups; and return `None` when selection or grouping is empty.
- In scope: String parsing for the six methods; single-index one-row Arrow results; multi-index one-row-per-instrument results; Boolean and every Arrow integer/float width; Pandas scalar integer widening; grouped narrow-integer preservation with overflow promotion; Float16/32 mean preservation; field and schema metadata retention; both index level orders; typed unknown-method/shape/type/selection errors; and live execution of the original Python function.
- Out of scope: Arbitrary Pandas attribute names, `method_kwargs`, offset-based single-index `first`/`last`, string/object concatenating reductions, callable `groupby.apply`, Python bindings, and physical dynamic plugin loading. - Compatibility decisions: Pandas scalar/Series/DataFrame unions are represented uniformly as Arrow `RecordBatch`: single-index reductions contain one value row without datetime; grouped reductions contain instrument plus values. Pandas `NaN` reduction results map to Arrow null where the output dtype is newly created, while first/last preserve an existing edge NaN exactly. Unknown dynamic strings fail explicitly instead of attempting reflection. Group integer results are first reduced in Int64/UInt64 and safely narrowed only if every group fits, matching Pandas overflow promotion.
- Plugin boundary: Built-in reductions are deterministic core operations and are not pluginized. Arbitrary callable aggregation is the next explicit extension point: an object-safe, batch-oriented trait should receive Arrow group batches and return versioned Arrow results. Cross-dylib loading must later use Arrow IPC/FFI with `abi_stable` or a Wasmtime component; raw Rust trait-object ABI is not promised.

Both are Apache-2.0, declare Rust 1.85 support, and match the existing Arrow 59.2.0 stack. Existing `arrow-ord` and `arrow-select` provide group ordering, take, filter, and concat. Polars/DataFusion were rejected for this slice because they add a dataframe/query stack without improving the narrow reduction contract.

## Time-series callable aggregation

- Contract: After stable time selection, call a custom aggregator once for a single datetime index or once per non-null instrument for a two-level index; preserve sorted group order and Pandas `group_keys=False`-style output shapes; pass keyword arguments; propagate callable failures; permit scalar-equivalent, multi-row, and zero-row results; and return `None` only when the selected source itself is empty.
- In scope: An object-safe `Send + Sync` `TimeSeriesAggregator` trait; declared Arrow output schemas; JSON-compatible ordered arguments; exact schema validation; framework-owned instrument-column insertion; multi-row and empty plugin outputs; typed schema/group/reserved-column/mismatch errors; a `ts_data_last`/`_ts_data_valid` adapter; and a benchmark `(x + 1).prod()` compounded-return adapter.
- Out of scope: Direct execution of arbitrary Python callable objects, Pandas object-dtype values, unrestricted Python truthiness for keyword values, preservation of arbitrary Pandas result-index subclasses, panic containment, plugin discovery, and a stable cross-process or native dynamic-library ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: The callable boundary uses `RecordBatch` uniformly instead of Python's scalar/Series/DataFrame union. A plugin declares its exact value schema before grouping and must omit the reserved instrument field for grouped inputs; the framework repeats each group key for every returned row and concatenates the batches. All-null instrument keys produce `Some(empty batch)`, while an empty selected source returns `None` without invoking the plugin. The bundled `last` adapter deliberately accepts only a JSON Boolean, providing a stable typed wire contract rather than Python's arbitrary-object truthiness.
- Plugin boundary: The trait is a compile-time dependency-injection boundary and is object-safe for in-process implementations, but it is not claimed as a Rust dylib ABI. A later physical plugin layer should version the Arrow schema and arguments and use Arrow IPC/FFI with `abi_stable`, or a Wasmtime component when sandboxing and failure isolation are required. Runtime-owned aggregator names use `Cow<str>` so adapters are not restricted to string literals.
- Dependencies: Reuse Apache Arrow 59.2.0 throughout: `arrow-select` supplies take/concat, `arrow-arith` supplies wrapping numeric addition and products, and `arrow-cast` supplies compatible widening. `serde_json` moved from test-only to the production dependency set for versionable JSON-compatible callable arguments. ## Cached NumpyQuote access

- Contract: Convert every quote value column to a NumPy-compatible Float64 matrix at construction; ignore frequency counts while accepting minute/day units; return `None` for a missing stock before validating bounds, region, field, or method; use Qlib's market-aware single-value shortcut; implement `sum`, `mean`, `last`, `all`, and `ts_data_last`; and cache successful results with Python's 512-entry LRU policy.

Float64 nulls become IEEE NaN so positional `last` preserves missingness, while `ts_data_last` uses the shared valid-value helper and returns `None` when every value is missing. Only successful `Result` values, including `None`, enter the cache; errors never do.

The single-value detector, Float64 compatibility rules, and LRU policy are deterministic core behavior and are not separately pluginized. Remote or physical plugin adapters should implement/version the `Quote` Arrow contract rather than expose Rust trait objects across a dylib ABI.

## Stock-indexed single metric operations

- Contract: Preserve stock-index order for scalar operations; sorted label union for arithmetic on differently labelled metrics; identical-label requirements for metric comparisons; Pandas missing-value propagation; `add(fill_value=...)` one-sided filling while retaining jointly missing values; Float64/Boolean reduction behavior; element-wise absolute value, replacement, callback application, and reindexing.
- In scope: The abstract storage boundary represented upstream by `BaseSingleMetric`; all behavior supplied by `SingleMetric`; the concrete `PandasSingleMetric` numeric/Boolean path; scalar and metric add/subtract/multiply/divide/equal/greater/less operations; reverse scalar operations; `len`, `empty`, `sum`, `mean`, `count`, `abs`, `add`, `replace`, `apply`, and `reindex`; typed errors; and live execution of the three original Python classes through AST extraction.
- Out of scope: `PandasOrderIndicator`, `NumpyOrderIndicator`, the separate `qlib.utils.index_data.SingleData` implementation used by the NumPy indicator path, arbitrary Pandas object/string dtypes, duplicate-index Cartesian alignment, Python operator overloading, PyO3 bindings, and runtime plugin discovery/loading. The authoritative Python module contains no `NumpySingleMetric` class; inventing one would create a false compatibility surface.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust normalizes numeric inputs to Arrow Float64 and represents Pandas/NumPy NaN as Arrow null; Boolean comparison results remain Arrow Boolean and convert missing comparisons to `false`, matching ordinary Pandas Series behavior. Differently labelled arithmetic sorts the union of stock identifiers, while identically labelled input retains left order. Duplicate stock identifiers are rejected explicitly because Qlib order indicators are stock-keyed and Pandas duplicate-label Cartesian alignment is not part of their observable consumer path.
- Plugin boundary: `SingleMetric: Send + Sync` is object-safe and exposes immutable Arrow index/value arrays. Framework-owned alignment and arithmetic accept `&dyn SingleMetric`, so alternative in-memory, IPC, remote, or future plugin-backed storage can participate without reimplementing Qlib semantics. This is a compile-time/runtime dependency-injection boundary, not a stable Rust dylib ABI; a physical plugin must version Arrow IPC/FFI or use an isolated component boundary.

## Order price advantage

- Contract: If the `trade_price` metric exists and is empty, replace `pa` with an empty metric without reading `trade_dir` or `base_price`; otherwise compute `(1 - 2 * trade_dir) * (trade_price / base_price - 1)`. Preserve sell/buy sign, backend ordering/alignment, missing-value propagation, IEEE NaN and signed infinity, and Python's required-metric evaluation order.
- In scope: `Indicator._agg_order_price_advantage`; NumPy same-stock-set alignment with reordered labels; Pandas sorted label union; empty overwrite; missing `trade_price`, `trade_dir`, and `base_price`; zero and infinite base/trade prices; NaN direction; equal-size and different-size dense mismatches; both concrete stores; and live AST execution of the original Python method and storage classes.
- Out of scope: Producing `base_price`/`base_volume`, Exchange queries, TWAP/VWAP selection, decision trade-range clipping, full outer aggregation orchestration, Python bindings, runtime plugin discovery, and physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: Dense computation first validates `trade_price` against `base_price`, then `trade_dir` against the ratio labels, matching Python expression evaluation; output follows `trade_dir` order. Pandas computes over the sorted union and uses NaN for absent labels. The live NumPy/Pandas path can differ by one final-bit rounding for finite ratios, so differential assertions permit exactly one `f64::EPSILON`; index order, NaN, and infinity remain exact. Rust's typed snapshots reject duplicate labels earlier than Pandas, consistent with the established store contract.
- Plugin boundary: The calculation reads and writes only Qlib-owned `MetricSnapshot` values through `IndicatorStoreAccess`; adapters select dense or Pandas alignment semantics through `IndicatorAggregationMode`. The formula remains framework-owned domain behavior, while any future Exchange or base-price plugin only needs to provide a validated `base_price` metric. The trait boundary is in-process dependency injection, not a stable native ABI; physical providers require versioned DTO/Arrow IPC or an isolated component/process boundary.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `BTreeSet`-based sorted union, `IndexMap` label lookup, Arrow-backed Pandas adapter, and ndarray-backed dense adapter are reused. Adding a dataframe or numerical crate would duplicate existing storage machinery for one Qlib-specific elementwise formula.

## Trade range rules

- Contract: `IdxTradeRange` returns its stored indices unchanged, including negative or reversed values, and does not support datetime clipping. `TradeRangeByTime` requires a strictly increasing closed clock range, anchors lookup and clipping to the relevant calendar date, delegates index resolution to the calendar provider, and preserves Python's same-day clipping behavior, including inverted output for a disjoint interval and same-day collapse for a cross-day request.
- In scope: `TradeRange`, `IdxTradeRange`, and `TradeRangeByTime`; object-safe calendar lookup; index and datetime clipping; minute, second, microsecond, date-only, naive datetime, and RFC 3339 clock parsing; missing-calendar, invalid-time, invalid-bounds, unsupported-clipping, and provider failures; exact provider-call assertions; and live AST execution of the original Python classes.
- Out of scope: `BaseTradeDecision`, `TradeCalendarManager` itself, complete calendar scheduling, `Exchange`, `_get_base_vol_pri`, base-price/base-volume production, timezone-retaining domain types, Python bindings, runtime discovery, and physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust exposes a typed trait rather than instantiating Python's abstract-style base class. Invalid strings and equal/reversed time bounds return typed errors instead of Pandas `DateParseError` and Python `AssertionError`. `Option<&dyn TradeCalendarRange>` retains the observable `None` behavior. Chrono covers the characterized common formats; Pandas' unbounded natural-language parser is deliberately not replicated, so a future Python adapter may normalize uncommon spellings before entering the Rust core. RFC 3339 offsets are projected to their written local clock, matching the observed Python `.time()` result. Upstream defines no serialization contract, so this slice adds none.
- Plugin boundary: object-safe `TradeCalendarRange: Send + Sync` exposes only the calendar start datetime and fallible range-index lookup. `TradeRange` is likewise object-safe, so decision code can accept custom in-process range rules without depending on a concrete calendar implementation. Provider errors remain typed and framework-visible. These Rust traits are dependency-injection seams, not a stable dylib ABI; physical plugins still require versioned DTOs and a process/component boundary.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `chrono` 0.4.45 supplies parsing and date/time arithmetic, and existing `thiserror` supplies public typed failures. Qlib's anchoring, index delegation, and clipping rules remain local because no general-purpose crate implements that domain contract.

## Base volume and price

- Contract: Optionally clip the requested timestamps through the decision trade range, request the direction-specific raw deal-price shape, discard every price that is not strictly greater than `1e-8`, and return no pair when prices are absent or fully filtered. TWAP gives every retained point unit weight. VWAP aligns raw volume to retained price timestamps, ignores NaN weights/products with NumPy `nansum` semantics, permits negative/zero/infinite values, and returns IEEE NaN or signed infinity when division requires it. Duplicate timestamps remain positional when both indices are exactly equal; reindexing otherwise uses the provider volume series' last duplicate value.
- In scope: `Indicator._get_base_vol_pri`; typed default/case-insensitive `twap`, `vwap`, and `deal_price` configuration; scalar and timestamp-series results; absent/empty data; strict threshold filtering; reordered, missing, scalar, NaN, duplicate, and zero-sum volumes; buy/sell direction forwarding; TradeRange clipping; provider and missing-volume failures; object-safe provider dispatch; and live AST execution of the original Python method and `SingleData` implementation.
- Out of scope: `Indicator._agg_base_price`, full `BaseTradeDecision`, concrete `Exchange` construction, quote-field selection/fallback logging, price expressions other than the currently implemented `deal_price`, serialization, Python bindings, runtime discovery, and physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: `MarketDataValue` replaces Python's runtime union of `int`/`float`/NumPy number/`SingleData`; unsupported runtime shapes cannot cross the typed core. `MarketDataSeries::try_new` rejects unequal buffers before provider use while deliberately allowing duplicate timestamps. An absent price maps to `Ok(None)`; absent VWAP volume is a typed `MissingVolume` error instead of Python's assertion. `BasePriceConfig::parse` validates source before aggregation and reports typed errors; unlike Python, a caller cannot defer an invalid aggregation until after an empty-price short circuit because valid configuration is established at the Rust boundary. This affects only the new Rust API, not an existing Python-facing adapter. Floating-point results retain exact IEEE behavior and the differential uses exact values for the characterized fixtures.
- Plugin boundary: object-safe `BasePriceDataProvider: Send + Sync` exposes only raw direction-aware deal prices and volumes using Qlib-owned `MarketDataValue`, `MarketDataSeries`, and `TimeRange` DTOs. `BasePriceRequest` packages the stock, interval, direction, optional `TradeRange`, and typed configuration without exposing Arrow, ndarray, Exchange, or backend error types. Provider failures remain typed. This is an in-process dependency-injection seam, not a stable dylib ABI; physical providers still require versioned DTO/Arrow IPC or a process/component boundary.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `strum` derives case-insensitive configuration parsing, `chrono` supplies typed timestamps, and `thiserror` supplies public failures. Existing Arrow/ndarray machinery was evaluated but is intentionally kept out of this narrow provider contract: two equal-length numeric buffers plus Qlib-specific duplicate/reindex/`nansum` rules do not justify leaking or adding a dataframe representation. Standard `HashMap` reproduces last-duplicate lookup during reindexing.

## Cross-step base-price aggregation

- Contract: Read the current `trade_dir` metric; if it is absent or empty, leave existing base metrics unchanged. Otherwise pair inner indicators and decision steps with Python `zip`, silently ignore either unmatched tail, reindex each step's `base_price` and `base_volume` to trade-direction order, and call the base-price provider only where price is NaN or missing. Existing non-NaN prices retain their accompanying volume, including NaN, zero, negative, or infinite values. Aggregate the sorted stock union with NumPy `nansum` semantics: sum volumes, sum price-times-volume, and divide even when the denominator is zero so IEEE NaN/infinity is preserved. A non-empty direction metric with zero paired steps overwrites both outputs with empty metrics.
- In scope: `Indicator._agg_base_price`; object-safe inner-store reads; `BasePriceStep`; exact `zip` truncation; missing metric fallback; stock reindexing; lazy direction conversion; TradeRange propagation; selective provider backfill; absent provider values; sorted union; multi-step weighted aggregation; both Numpy and Pandas output adapters; empty/no-pair behavior; atomic provider, TradeRange, direction, and VWAP-volume failures; and live execution against both original Python storage backends.
- Out of scope: Full `Indicator.agg_order_indicators` orchestration, complete `BaseTradeDecision`, concrete `Exchange`/Quote adapters, Exchange price-field fallback logging, physical plugin loading, Python bindings, and trade-indicator summary orchestration.
- Compatibility decisions: Missing inner `base_price` or `base_volume` metrics become empty snapshots and therefore reindex to NaN, matching `get_index_data` rather than producing `MissingMetric`. Direction conversion is deliberately lazy: NaN or another non-enum number is harmless when an existing price avoids lookup, but becomes typed `InvalidDirection` when provider lookup is required. Only exact numeric 0/1 cross the typed `OrderDir` boundary, matching real `Exchange.get_deal_price`; a custom Python Exchange that accepts arbitrary directions could behave differently. All provider and validation work completes before either output assignment, preserving failure atomicity. `MetricSnapshot` continues to reject duplicate stock identifiers earlier than Python, while step ordering, final sorted union, missing-value behavior, and IEEE results remain compatible.
- Plugin boundary: Inner indicators are accepted as `&dyn IndicatorStoreAccess`, so a single aggregation can read heterogeneous in-process storage plugins without coupling to Arrow or ndarray. Each `BasePriceStep` contains only Chrono timestamps and an optional object-safe `TradeRange`; missing-price lookup reuses the Qlib-owned `BasePriceDataProvider` and DTOs. Output remains generic over the selected `IndicatorStore`. These traits are in-process dependency-injection seams, not a stable dylib ABI; cross-process plugins still need versioned DTO/Arrow IPC or a component protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `indexmap` preserves per-step insertion order, `chrono` supplies step timestamps, and `thiserror` supplies the aggregate error union. Existing standard `BTreeSet` and `HashMap` helpers provide deterministic sorted union and label lookup. Arrow, ndarray, and Polars were not added to the orchestration layer because the established store adapters already own backend conversion and the remaining weighted union is small Qlib-specific domain logic.

## Full order-indicator orchestration

- Contract: Run aggregate trade information, replace outer target amounts, align and calculate fulfillment rates, aggregate cross-step base prices, and calculate price advantage in exactly that order. The pipeline is intentionally non-atomic: each completed stage remains visible when a later stage fails, and the first stage mutates every successfully processed inner `trade_price` metric into signed traded notional. Fulfillment-rate output follows outer `amount` labels, treats missing or NaN deals as zero, and retains IEEE NaN/infinity from division. Empty inputs install empty trade/amount/fulfillment/price-advantage metrics while leaving old base-price metrics unchanged because the base-price stage short-circuits on empty direction.
- In scope: `Indicator.agg_order_indicators`; public typed `OrderIndicatorAggregationConfig`; the aggregate error union; standalone label-aligned fulfillment-rate recomputation; exact stage and error ordering; mutable inner stores; typed outer orders; `BasePriceStep`; `BasePriceDataProvider`; TWAP configuration forwarding; normal and empty operation; base-provider failure partial state; final dense alignment failure; Pandas missing-base union behavior; both concrete stores; and live AST execution of the complete original Python method chain.
- Out of scope: Constructing `BaseTradeDecision`, extracting steps from executor decisions, a concrete `Exchange` adapter, quote-field fallback selection, trade-summary calculation, Python bindings, serialization/versioning, process isolation, runtime discovery, and stable physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: The Rust entry accepts the already-normalized outer order slice and step DTOs rather than Python decision objects. Python's open dictionary is represented by the exact typed `pa_config` subset; unrelated keys are absent by construction. As established in the base-price slice, invalid configuration cannot be deferred past an empty-price short circuit because Rust validates configuration at the boundary. The full pipeline computes fulfillment rate directly from metrics guaranteed by its two preceding stages, while the public standalone method returns `MissingMetric` for independently malformed state. Dense output still requires identical price/base labels and can fail only after base metrics are committed; Pandas instead succeeds over its sorted label union with NaN values.
- Plugin boundary: The orchestration owns domain order and partial-state semantics. Storage remains replaceable through `IndicatorStore`, with Arrow-backed Pandas and ndarray-backed dense implementations exercising the same entry point. Market lookup remains replaceable through object-safe `BasePriceDataProvider`, and trade-range clipping through object-safe `TradeRange`. The typed config and DTOs keep provider/storage dependencies out of the orchestration. These are in-process dependency-injection seams, not a stable native ABI; dynamically loaded or cross-process plugins still require versioned DTO/Arrow IPC or a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. The slice deliberately reuses the existing third-party stack: `indexmap` for Python-compatible order, `chrono` for step timestamps, `thiserror` for the public stage error union, `strum` for previously typed configuration, Arrow for the Pandas store, and ndarray for the dense store. Adding Polars or another dataframe/numerical crate would duplicate the established adapters for a sequencing-only layer.

## Exchange quote provider adapter

- Contract: Normalize a shared deal-price field by adding the Qlib `$` prefix, preserve explicitly directional fields unchanged, select the sell or buy field from `OrderDir`, and delegate to `Quote`. A raw selection (`method=None` in Python, `QuoteMethod::Selection` in Rust) returns the original scalar/series without close-price fallback. For aggregated methods, `None`, NaN, and values at or below `1e-8` fall back to `$close` with the same method and emit two warnings; a value immediately above the threshold and positive infinity do not fall back. Volume always queries `$volume` and preserves the requested method. Arrow timestamp/value series are converted to the narrow `MarketDataValue` DTO used by base-price aggregation.
- In scope: The characterized subset of `Exchange.__init__`, `get_deal_price`, and `get_volume`; `DealPriceFields`; direction-aware `ExchangeQuoteProvider`; raw and aggregated quote calls; close fallback and warning emission; object-safe `Quote` dispatch; `ArrowQuote` and `NumpyQuote` integration; implementation of `BasePriceDataProvider`; scalar and timestamp-series conversion; second/millisecond/microsecond/nanosecond Arrow timestamps; timezone metadata; malformed shapes/types/null timestamps/out-of-range timestamps; provider errors; direct `Indicator.get_base_volume_price` TWAP/VWAP integration; and a live Python AST differential.
- Out of scope: Full `Exchange` construction and data subscription, price-limit/cost/order-execution behavior, factor and close APIs beyond the characterized fallback, full decisions/executors, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, and stable physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: A typed directional constructor requires exactly two fields, so Python tuple/list length errors are unrepresentable. `OrderDir` makes unsupported direction integers unrepresentable. An empty shared field returns typed `EmptySharedDealPrice` instead of Python `IndexError`. Raw requests deliberately never apply fallback, matching the base-price workflow. Arrow timezone metadata is interpreted as a physical instant and projected to naive UTC because the current domain DTO is timezone-free. Malformed plugin shapes and values return typed adapter errors rather than downstream Python/Arrow exceptions.
- Plugin boundary: `ExchangeQuoteProvider` owns `Arc<dyn Quote>`, so `ArrowQuote`, `NumpyQuote`, and custom in-process quote implementations can be injected without changing base-price orchestration. The framework retains direction selection, fallback thresholds, warning policy, and Arrow-to-domain validation; plugins supply market data only. `BasePriceDataProvider` remains the narrower domain-facing boundary. These Rust trait objects are not a stable dylib ABI; physical or cross-process plugins require versioned DTOs, Arrow IPC, or a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: Added `tracing` 0.1.44 with default features disabled and only `std` enabled for library-safe warning events; it is MIT-licensed, declares Rust 1.65, and is compatible with the workspace Rust 1.85 baseline. Subscriber configuration stays with the application. The implementation reuses existing `Arc`, Apache Arrow casting, Chrono timestamp conversion, `thiserror`, and the existing `Quote` implementations. Polars or another dataframe crate was not added because Arrow already represents the plugin result and the target DTO is intentionally narrow. Dependency inspection introduced no unexplained duplicate major versions; the remaining `syn` 2/3 split is proc-macro tooling.

## Typed order trade decisions

- Contract: Store concrete decision items in producer order with mutable-list and replacement access; capture the closed strategy-step interval and optional shared trade range; and distinguish an omitted range fallback from an explicitly supplied range or `None`. `OrderTradeDecision` fills only missing order start/end timestamps from the captured interval, preserves supplied endpoints and execution state, exposes validated orders, and is non-empty only when at least one amount is strictly greater than `1e-6`. `EmptyTradeDecision` always exposes no items and remains empty. Decision ranges propagate by shared identity only when the inner decision has no range. Range limits preserve raw negative/reversed indices until `total_step` is known, then clip only when `start < 0` or `end >= total_step`, including Python's `(0, -1)` result at zero total steps.
- In scope: The dependency-ready subset of `BaseTradeDecision`, `EmptyTradeDecision`, and `TradeDecisionWO`; generic non-order decision storage; typed order extraction; stable order/item mutation and replacement; missing-time normalization; the strict empty threshold including nextafter, negative, and NaN amounts; captured start/end metadata; optional `total_step`; omitted/tuple/`None` range fallbacks; range provider success/failure; Python-compatible clipping and warnings; shared range propagation; `BasePriceStep` projection; object-safe `OrderDecision`; and a live AST differential against the original Python classes.
- Out of scope: Retaining a concrete Python/Rust strategy object; `BaseTradeDecision.update` and the strategy update hook; `get_data_cal_range_limit` and global data-calendar lookup; `TradeDecisionWithDetails`; exact Python `repr` text and object addresses; executor initialization/execution; serial/parallel order iteration; Python/PyO3 bindings; serialization; process isolation; and stable physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: `TradeDecision<T>` retains Qlib's generic non-order container capability, while executor/report APIs can require `TradeDecision<Order>` or `dyn OrderDecision`; a non-order value therefore cannot cross the order boundary and Python's constructor/extraction `AssertionError` becomes unrepresentable. Rust takes the captured step timestamps explicitly and uses them once; Python `TradeDecisionWO` reads the strategy calendar twice (base metadata, then order defaults), which is observable only for a stateful/non-deterministic calendar and is deliberately not reproduced before the strategy/calendar layer exists. Returned vectors remain mutable, but caller mutations after construction are not automatically time-normalized, matching Python list mutation after `__init__`. Missing-calendar range errors use the explicit fallback when present; other typed provider failures propagate. Warning delivery uses `tracing` instead of a hard-wired logger.
- Plugin boundary: `OrderDecision: Send + Sync` exposes only an order slice, captured timestamps, optional `TradeRange`, the Qlib empty rule, and `BasePriceStep` projection. Executors and report adapters can therefore consume custom in-process decision providers without depending on a concrete strategy implementation. `SharedTradeRange = Arc<dyn TradeRange>` preserves propagation identity and shares existing range plugins. `TradeDecision<T>` itself remains framework-owned mutable state. These Rust traits are not a stable dylib ABI; physical/cross-process decisions require versioned order/range DTOs or a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Chrono supplies timestamps, `thiserror` preserves typed range failures, and `tracing` emits clipping warnings. `Arc` and `Infallible` come from the standard library. A collection or plugin-registry crate would add no capability: stable sequence/mutation is exactly `Vec`, and Qlib's threshold, fallback-presence, clipping, and range-propagation rules are small domain contracts that require local compatibility code.

## Simulator order iteration

- Contract: Extract decision-owned orders into a new independently reorderable batch while retaining references to the original mutable order objects. `serial` preserves the exact strategy sequence. `parallel` is not concurrent execution: it performs a stable buy-first sort, so all buys precede sells while relative order within each direction is unchanged. Neither mode mutates the decision's stored sequence. Empty decisions return an empty batch. Mode matching is exact and case-sensitive, and extraction occurs before an unsupported-mode error.
- In scope: `_retrieve_orders_from_decision`; `SimulatorExecutor.TT_SERIAL`, `TT_PARAL`, and `_get_order_iterator`; object-safe mutable order extraction; new-container/same-order mutation semantics; serial order; mixed-direction stable parallel ordering; same-direction stability; original decision-order preservation; empty `EmptyTradeDecision`; exact string parsing/rendering; unsupported text and extraction/error ordering; tuple-returning Python decisions in the differential; non-order Python assertion ordering; and live AST execution of the original helper and method.
- Out of scope: `SimulatorExecutor.__init__` infrastructure, `_collect_data`, step/day state, `Exchange.deal_order`, volume/cash/position clipping, account mutation, execution-result tuples, verbosity/printing, asynchronous or genuinely parallel execution, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, and physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust returns `Vec<&mut Order>`: the vector is a fresh list-like container that can be reordered without changing the decision, while mutations update the decision-owned order, matching Python's new list of shared object references. `OrderDecision::orders_mut` extends the in-process boundary for later execution-result mutation and Rust's exclusive borrow prevents concurrent aliases during a batch. Non-order items cannot cross this typed boundary, replacing Python's per-item `AssertionError`; a Python tuple/generator adapter must first normalize values into a typed decision slice. The public Rust entry accepts text, so Python's unsupported `None`/integer modes are unrepresentable after adapter validation. Invalid text still requests the mutable slice before parsing, preserving observable call/error order for custom in-process providers.
- Plugin boundary: `dyn OrderDecision` remains the replaceable in-process decision source and now exposes both immutable and exclusive mutable order slices. The iterator owns only the temporary vector of references; sorting policy remains framework-owned so a plugin cannot silently change serial/parallel semantics. The boundary is infallible because upstream's concrete `get_decision` path is infallible; fallible remote providers must validate/materialize a batch before entering it. Rust trait objects and borrowed references are not a stable dylib/wire ABI, so physical plugins require versioned owned order DTOs plus explicit result write-back.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `strum` derives exact enum parsing, display, string access, and variant inventory. The standard library's stable `sort_by_key` plus `Reverse` implements Qlib's buy-first stable ordering. A parallelism crate such as Rayon would be semantically wrong because Python only reorders sequential execution; a collection crate would add no value over the required temporary `Vec`.

## Exchange execution sizing

- Contract: Adjusted-price mode or a missing trade unit bypasses factor lookup; otherwise an explicit factor takes priority over market lookup. Market lookup requires stock and both timestamps, queries `$factor` with last-valid aggregation, and rejects a missing result. A trade unit represents `trade_unit / factor`. Amount rounding preserves Python's exact `(deal_amount * factor + 0.1) // trade_unit * trade_unit / factor` evaluation order and CPython float-floor-division correction. Cash-limited buy sizing preserves the minimum-fee threshold, proportional-fee branch, fixed-fee branch, comparison order, and IEEE NaN/infinity behavior.
- In scope: `_get_factor_or_raise_error`, `get_amount_of_trade_unit`, `round_amount_by_trade_unit`, and `_get_buy_amount_by_cash_limit`; direct/provider factor precedence; adjusted and disabled trade-unit short circuits; incomplete market keys; missing/failing factor providers; zero, negative, NaN, infinity, and signed-zero factors; positive/negative/zero trade units; CPython floor-division correction; exact `f64` bit checks; cash below minimum cost; both fee branches and their equality boundary; zero/negative/NaN/infinite cash, price, cost ratio, and minimum cost; `ExchangeQuoteProvider` scalar/missing/series/failure integration; and live AST execution of the four original Python methods.
- Out of scope: `_clip_amount_by_volume`, price-limit checks, `_calc_trade_info_by_order`, sell-position clipping, execution-cost calculation beyond buy sizing, order mutation, account updates, full `Exchange` construction, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, and stable physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust reports explicit typed errors for missing lookup inputs/provider/value and for every divisor that Python would reject, while preserving the original operation order so an error occurs only on the same reached branch. Negative and non-finite values remain accepted wherever Python accepts them. Direct factors prevent provider calls. Provider series are rejected as an aggregated-factor shape error. Rust's native `f64::floor` is insufficient for Python `float //`; the private helper follows CPython's divmod sign adjustment, signed-zero rule, and quotient correction, including an extreme regression vector that reaches the otherwise rare correction branch.
- Plugin boundary: `FactorProvider: Send + Sync` is an object-safe, narrow in-process seam returning an optional scalar factor. `ExchangeExecutionSizer` accepts `Arc<dyn FactorProvider>`, while `ExchangeQuoteProvider` implements the trait through its existing `Arc<dyn Quote>` backend. The framework retains lookup validation, factor precedence, sizing, rounding, and fee policy; plugins only supply factors. These Rust traits are not a stable dylib ABI, so physical or cross-process plugins still require versioned DTOs and an explicit component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Chrono represents lookup timestamps, `thiserror` defines the typed public error surface, and Apache Arrow remains behind `ExchangeQuoteProvider` for quote shape/value conversion. Standard `Arc` provides provider ownership. No numerical or dataframe crate implements CPython's exact float `//` compatibility contract; the small CPython-derived algorithm is therefore local and isolated instead of adding an approximate dependency. Dependency inspection still shows only the explained `syn` 2/3 proc-macro split.

## Exchange volume clipping

- Contract: Select buy or sell limits from the order direction. If that directional configuration is absent, return the current `deal_amount` without querying market data or mutating the order. For configured limits, query every entry in source order: `current` uses `sum`, while `cum` uses `ts_data_last` and subtracts the stock's previously dealt amount. Apply Python's order-sensitive `min` across capacities, then `max(min(capacity, original), 0)`, mutate only after all lookups and validations succeed, emit a debug event only when the minimum capacity is strictly below the original amount, and return `None` after applying limits.
- In scope: `_clip_amount_by_volume`; typed current/cumulative modes and stable spellings; buy/sell selection; absent versus explicitly empty limit lists; object-safe provider dispatch; exact field/method call order; multiple-limit minimum selection; cumulative prior-fill subtraction; mutation and return semantics; provider/missing-value/missing-history failures and atomicity; negative values, positive/negative infinity, NaN in each ordering, NaN original/prior fill, positive and negative zero; debug-event execution; `ExchangeQuoteProvider` scalar/missing/series/failure adaptation; and live AST execution of the original Python method.
- Out of scope: `_get_vol_limit` parsing of Python tuple/dict objects, quote subscription-field collection, `check_stock_limit`, `_calc_trade_info_by_order`, impact/open/close cost calculation, position and cash clipping, trade-unit rounding composition, `deal_order`, account mutation, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, and stable physical plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: `Option<Vec<VolumeLimit>>` deliberately preserves Python's distinction between no configuration and a configured empty list. `VolumeLimitKind::from_python_name` rejects unsupported modes at the typed boundary instead of retaining an invalid tuple until execution; valid execution ordering is unchanged. Missing provider values, cumulative history, aggregated series, and quote failures become typed errors while preserving pre-mutation atomicity and the relevant provider-call order. Rust does not use `f64::min/max`, whose NaN behavior differs; explicit ordered comparisons reproduce Python built-ins, including first-NaN retention and negative-zero preservation. Typed `OrderDir` makes Python's fallback of every non-buy integer to sell unrepresentable after input validation.
- Plugin boundary: `VolumeLimitProvider: Send + Sync` accepts a stock, optional-bounded `TimeRange`, and typed `VolumeLimit`, returning an optional scalar. `ExchangeVolumeLimiter` owns an optional `Arc<dyn VolumeLimitProvider>` and keeps direction policy, aggregation meaning, cumulative subtraction, minimum selection, logging, and order mutation inside the framework. `ExchangeQuoteProvider` implements the seam over its existing `Arc<dyn Quote>` and private scalar validator. This is an in-process Rust trait, not a stable dylib/wire ABI; physical plugins still require versioned DTOs and an explicit component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No production or test dependency was added. Existing Apache Arrow and `Quote` perform market-data aggregation and scalar conversion, `thiserror` supplies typed errors, Chrono is carried by `TimeRange`, and `tracing` emits the debug event. A tiny test-only `tracing::Subscriber` fake verifies event execution without adding a subscriber implementation to the dependency graph. Collection and ordered-float crates were rejected because Qlib requires input-order `Vec` traversal and Python-specific raw `f64` NaN/signed-zero comparisons; those are short domain compatibility rules rather than general numerical infrastructure.

## Exchange order trade-info calculation

- Contract: Reproduce `Exchange._calc_trade_info_by_order` in its observable Python evaluation order: retrieve direction-specific price and summed volume, compute the unadjusted market value, retrieve and store the factor, initialize and volume-clip the deal amount, calculate quadratic impact, clip sells against holdings/cash or buys against cash, apply trade-unit rounding at the original branch point, then calculate the final value and fee. Provider and state failures retain exactly the order mutations already reached. Python's order-sensitive `min`/`max`, asymmetric `numpy.isclose`, NaN/infinity, signed zero, and the `1e-5` final-cost threshold remain explicit compatibility rules.
- In scope: Price/volume/factor lookup and ordering; built-in `ExchangeQuoteProvider` adaptation; bounded factor lookup and absent-stock behavior; factor and deal-amount mutation boundaries; composition with the completed volume limiter and execution sizer; buy with no position, insufficient cost cash, partial cash, and sufficient cash; sell with absent/missing/exact/near/limited/non-finite holdings; cash and position-provider failures; impact adjustment for finite, zero, NaN, and infinite total volume; open/close/minimum fee calculation; logging branches; typed errors; object-safe dispatch; and live AST execution of the original Python method.

- Compatibility decisions: The calculator deliberately mutates factor and the initial full deal amount before volume, sizing, or position failures because upstream has the same partial-mutation boundary. Missing price/volume and market failures remain pre-mutation. A sell without a position does not round, including when factor is absent; a buy always reaches rounding unless cash first clips it to zero. The built-in factor adapter requires both time bounds and returns `None` for stocks outside `Quote.get_all_stock`, matching upstream without weakening the more general plugin trait. Rust uses local ordered comparisons instead of `f64::min/max`, and `partial_cmp` plus the NumPy tolerance expression reproduces equality for signed zero and equal infinities while rejecting NaN and unequal non-finite values.
- Plugin boundary: `ExecutionMarketProvider: Send + Sync` supplies only deal price, summed market volume, and factor. `ExecutionPosition: Send + Sync` exposes read-only stock existence, held amount, and tradable cash. `ExchangeTradeCalculator` retains sequencing, mutations, impact/cost policy, volume-limit composition, and sizing policy, so provider plugins cannot silently redefine execution semantics. `ExchangeQuoteProvider` is the default market adapter. These are in-process Rust trait objects; versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol are still required for a stable dylib or remote plugin ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `thiserror` provides typed public failures, `tracing` carries diagnostic events, Chrono-backed `TimeRange` carries interval bounds, and Apache Arrow remains isolated behind `ExchangeQuoteProvider`. Existing framework-owned `ExchangeExecutionSizer` and `ExchangeVolumeLimiter` are composed rather than duplicated. A numerical crate was not added because the required behavior is CPython/NumPy-specific evaluation order over raw `f64`, and generic decimal/ordered-float abstractions would change NaN, infinity, signed-zero, or rounding behavior.

## Simulator execution collection

- Contract: Reproduce the synchronous execution loop in `SimulatorExecutor._collect_data`. Read the calendar once before obtaining the order iterator and once before every deal; derive the current naive calendar day from each per-order step start; replace the cumulative-fill map only when no day is recorded or the observed day is later; pass the current per-stock cumulative fills into the dealer; append `(order, value, cost, price)` in execution order; then add the order's mutated `deal_amount`, including a zero fill. Same-day and older timestamps retain the map. Errors stop immediately and preserve every calendar read, day transition, order mutation, and fill update already reached. The returned execution result and `trade_info` expose the same owned result allocation through shared slice views.
- In scope: Empty, serial, and buy-first parallel decisions; initial and per-order calendar reads; same-day, later-day, older-day, and restored no-day state; cumulative fill snapshots and rollover replacement; successful execution ordering and shared result storage; first/second deal failures; initial/per-order calendar failures; iterator validation failures after the initial calendar read; verbose gating; cash lookup; exact normal-value log formatting; reporter failures after fill accounting; direct object-safe dispatch; composition with the real `ExchangeDealExecutor`; and a live AST differential against the original Python loop.
- Out of scope: The broader `BaseExecutor.collect_data` lifecycle, nested generator delegation, range-limit validation, settlement, `update_bar_end`, calendar stepping, concrete account/position persistence, a framework-owned stdout sink, timezone-aware calendar identity, asynchronous execution, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, process isolation, and a stable physical plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `level` remains accepted but unused, matching this concrete Python method. A fresh `HashMap` replaces the prior map on rollover instead of clearing it, preserving replacement semantics for state observers internal to the collector. The structured reporter is called only after fill accumulation and cash retrieval, so position, cash, and reporter failures retain the upstream mutation boundary. Rust's typed decision boundary has already normalized Python's arbitrary iterable/non-order cases. `NaiveDateTime::date` preserves day-floor behavior but deliberately does not retain a Python timestamp's timezone identity. The formatter preserves the characterized message for ordinary finite values; Python-specific exotic float spelling remains a future binding-edge concern.
- Plugin boundary: `SimulatorCalendar: Send + Sync` supplies step intervals; `SimulatorDealProvider: Send + Sync` performs a deal from the current cumulative-fill snapshot, with `ExchangeDealExecutor` as the built-in adapter; and `SimulatorExecutionReporter: Send + Sync` receives a structured successful execution plus cash when verbose reporting is enabled. `SimulatorCollector` retains ordering, rollover, state mutation, and error policy so plugins cannot redefine loop semantics. These are in-process Rust trait objects, not stable dylib/wire interfaces; physical and remote plugins require versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Chrono provides timestamp/day handling, `thiserror` provides typed failures, and the standard library supplies `Arc` and `HashMap`. The completed decision iterator and exchange deal executor are composed rather than duplicated. Rayon or an async runtime would be semantically wrong because Qlib's `parallel` mode is only stable buy-first ordering followed by sequential execution; a plugin registry or collection crate adds no value to this slice.

These traits are in-process interfaces; stable physical/remote plugins still require versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Chrono represents closed bar timestamps, `thiserror` provides typed stage failures, and the standard library provides `Arc`. ## Position cash settlement

- Contract: Model the finite position's `cash`, optional `cash_delay`, and exact `_settle_type` fields. `"None"` is inactive and can be started repeatedly without changing a residual delayed-cash entry. Starting `"cash"` requires no active transaction and replaces any existing delay with positive zero. Sell proceeds use the exact `trade_value - cost` expression and enter delayed cash only during cash settlement, available cash when settlement is disabled, or fail for an unknown active type. Purchase payment always uses `cash -= trade_value + cost`. Committing cash adds the delay, removes it, and resets the type; disabled commit is a no-op; unknown or missing-delay commits retain all state. Infinite-position cash remains positive infinity and ignores every operation.
- In scope: `BasePosition.ST_NO`, `BasePosition.ST_CASH`; `Position.settle_start`, `settle_commit`, `get_cash`; the cash portions of `_buy_stock` and `_sell_stock`; normal and restored state; residual delay while inactive; repeated disabled starts; cash-delay overwrite; nested rejection; unknown settlement acceptance-at-start and deferred failure; missing restored delay; available versus settlement-inclusive cash; finite, NaN, positive-infinite, and negative-infinite arithmetic; purchase during settlement; `InfPosition` cash and settlement no-ops; typed errors; and live AST execution of the original Python methods.
- Out of scope: Stock dictionary construction, `_init_stock`, holdings amount mutation/deletion, NumPy `isclose`, oversell validation, order-direction dispatch, stock prices/counts/weights, total portfolio value, `ExecutionPosition`/`ExecutionTarget` implementation, concrete `Account`, bar-end metrics, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, process isolation, and a stable physical plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `PositionCash::restore` explicitly represents Python dictionaries/checkpoints that contain a residual `cash_delay` or inconsistent active state; normal construction starts without a delay. A cash state missing its delay returns `MissingDelayedCash`, the typed equivalent of Python's `KeyError`, and retains the transaction. Unknown strings are deliberately stored by `settle_start` and rejected only by sale or commit. `record_sale_proceeds` assumes holdings were already mutated, so its error cannot roll them back, matching `_sell_stock` ordering. Raw `f64` arithmetic preserves NaN, infinity, signed-zero, and operation order. `InfinitePositionCash` uses a separate zero-sized type rather than burdening every finite operation with an infinity branch.
- Plugin boundary: This slice is framework-owned state rather than replaceable infrastructure. It composes beneath the existing object-safe `AtomicExecutorAccount` and future concrete `ExecutionPosition`/`ExecutionTarget` adapter; custom accounts remain free to implement those traits without using `PositionCash`. Keeping the cash ledger concrete prevents plugins from silently redefining Qlib settlement arithmetic, while the surrounding account boundary remains replaceable.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `thiserror` represents typed settlement failures and the standard library supplies IEEE-754 `f64` operations. A decimal crate would change upstream NaN/infinity/signed-zero behavior; a transaction/state-machine crate would add substantially more abstraction than this small Qlib-specific protocol; and synchronization belongs to the owning account adapter rather than this mutable value object.

## Finite position order updates

- Contract: Reproduce the holdings and cash mutation core of Python `Position`. Construction normalizes a numeric holding to an amount-only record and preserves complete restored records. A buy computes amount before mutation, accumulates an existing amount without replacing its metadata, or inserts a new holding with price and zero weight, then pays cash. A sell computes amount first, requires the stock, deletes the complete holding when NumPy `isclose` matches, otherwise subtracts before validating oversell, and only then records proceeds through the settlement ledger. Errors retain exactly the mutations already reached.

Holdings and settlement remain framework-owned domain state rather than pluggable arithmetic. Existing third-party `indexmap` provides deterministic owned holdings and efficient keyed mutation/removal, while existing `thiserror` provides typed public failures. ## Position state and valuation

- Contract: Complete the locally computable `Position` state surface. Price, `count_<bar>`, and weight updates require an existing holding and mutate only the requested field. Missing counts read as zero. Stock value is accumulated from amount times price in holding order; total value adds available plus delayed cash. Amount and calculated-weight snapshots retain deterministic holding order. Stock-only weights divide by stock value, total weights divide by total account value, an empty position returns an empty map even with zero value, and a nonempty zero-valued denominator is a typed Python-compatible division failure. `update_weight_all` calculates the complete map before mutating any stored weight. `InfPosition` preserves its no-op price update, infinite stock value, NaN price, and explicit unsupported collection/total-value operations.

Python rebuilds its stock list through a `set` on every call, so floating accumulation order is hash-dependent; Rust deliberately retains deterministic insertion order. The live differential therefore permits exactly one ULP only for finite numeric leaves affected by this nondeterminism, while structures, errors, empty results, NaN/infinity markers, and all other values remain exact. Python float division by positive or negative zero becomes `ZeroPositionValue`; the empty-map short circuit is preserved. Calculated weights are staged before mutation, preserving upstream failure atomicity.
- Plugin boundary: Valuation and holding metadata remain framework-owned domain semantics inside concrete `Position`; making arithmetic pluggable would allow an adapter to redefine account value. The already completed `ExecutionPosition`/`ExecutionTarget` traits remain the replaceable exchange/simulator seam, and `InfinitePosition` supplies its alternate implementation. `fill_stock_value` is intentionally deferred behind a future market-data provider because it performs infrastructure I/O rather than local position arithmetic. Stable physical/remote plugins still require versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party `indexmap` stores both holdings and arbitrary normalized count fields with deterministic order; existing `thiserror` supplies typed errors. A DataFrame/Arrow dependency is unnecessary until `fill_stock_value`; a decimal or ordered-float crate would alter Qlib's IEEE-754 NaN, infinity, signed-zero, and division behavior. The small one-ULP comparator is test-only compatibility logic, not production numerical infrastructure.

## Account order accounting

- Contract: Reproduce `AccumulatedInfo` and the order-facing core of `Account`. Return without cost, cost, and turnover are independent cumulative `f64` fields with exact reset-to-positive-zero behavior. Every order first checks `current_position.skip_update`; an infinite/skipped position causes a no-op. With portfolio metrics disabled, the position still updates but no cumulative field changes. A sell adds turnover and cost, validates/divides by trade price, reads the pre-sale holding price, adds `trade_value - stock_price * trade_amount`, and only then mutates the position. A buy mutates the position first, then adds turnover/cost and `stock_price * trade_amount - trade_value`. Every failure retains all state reached before it.
- In scope: Accumulated state construction, getters, incremental updates, reset, and NaN/infinities; portfolio-metrics and infinite-position short circuits; finite buy/sell composition; existing-position buy price behavior; read-only execution view; `ExecutionTarget` implementation; sell price, zero-price, oversell, and position-write failures; buy position-write and post-write zero-price failures; arbitrary plugin view/read/write failures; exact plugin call order; and live AST execution of the original Python methods.
- Out of scope: Full `Account.__init__` configuration discovery, frequency and benchmark reset, `fill_stock_value`, cash settlement delegation, quote-driven `update_current_position`, portfolio metrics, historical positions, indicators, `update_bar_end`, nested-account shallow copying, Python/PyO3 bindings, serialization, runtime discovery, process isolation, and a stable physical plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Typed `OrderDir` removes Python's invalid raw-direction surface. Rust explicitly rejects positive and negative zero before division because native `f64` division would otherwise return infinity; the rejection occurs at the same mutation point as Python `ZeroDivisionError`. NaN and infinities retain raw IEEE-754 evaluation order. Missing prices and mutation failures become typed `AccountPositionError` values with stable messages. A boxed trait object replaces Python's dynamically configured `BasePosition`; nested-executor sharing and shallow-copy identity are deferred until the history/nested-account slice. The outer `skip_update` call and the second short-circuited metrics check are both preserved because custom Python positions can observe them.
- Plugin boundary: `AccountPosition: Send + Sync` exposes only skip policy, a read-only `ExecutionPosition` view, latest-price access, and execution mutation. `Position` and `InfinitePosition` are the built-in adapters. `Account` retains direction sequencing and cumulative arithmetic, then implements the existing `ExecutionTarget` seam consumed by `ExchangeDealExecutor`; a plugin can supply storage or transport but cannot silently reorder account accounting. These are in-process Rust traits, not a stable dylib/wire ABI; physical or remote plugins still require versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `thiserror` provides account and adapter failures, while the standard library supplies boxed trait objects and IEEE-754 arithmetic. `Position`, `InfinitePosition`, `ExecutionPosition`, and `ExecutionTarget` are composed rather than duplicated. A decimal crate would change upstream special-value behavior, and an async runtime, transaction framework, or plugin registry would add infrastructure without matching this synchronous failure-retaining protocol.

## Account current-position bar update

- Contract: At each bar end, an infinite/skip-update position returns before stock enumeration or market access. A finite position snapshots its current stock identifiers in position order, checks suspension for each stock over the exact closed timestamp range, skips close lookup and mutation for suspended stocks, otherwise reads the last-valid `$close` and immediately replaces that stock's price. Only after every stock succeeds does the account increment every holding's `count_<freq>`. The empty finite position still reaches the count operation. Any failure stops at its exact stage, retains earlier price mutations, and prevents the final count increment.
- In scope: Account frequency storage and default `"day"`; explicit-frequency and boxed constructors; deterministic stock-list snapshots; close-price mutation; all-holding count increment; infinite-position short circuit; empty holdings; suspension and close lookups; timestamp and frequency forwarding; missing close and quote errors; every position/market plugin failure stage; earlier-mutation retention; `ExchangeQuoteProvider` adaptation; and live AST execution of the original Python `Account.update_current_position` method.
- Out of scope: `PortfolioMetrics`, account-value/return calculations, historical deep-copy snapshots, `now_account_value`, weight refresh orchestration, indicator updates, complete `update_bar_end`, Python/PyO3 bindings, wire-format versioning, runtime plugin discovery, process isolation, and a stable physical plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `AccountPosition::stock_ids` returns an owned ordered snapshot so later price mutations cannot invalidate iteration and so remote adapters can eventually map it to an owned DTO. `TimeRange` carries the exact required start/end timestamps. `AccountBarMarket::close` returns a required `f64`; the built-in exchange adapter converts an absent last-valid close into a typed error because Rust cannot pass Python's runtime `None` through a numeric position API, while the preceding suspension check makes this an inconsistent-provider case. NaN remains a valid `f64` at the generic plugin boundary and is stored unchanged. Existing constructors retain a `"day"` default, while explicit-frequency constructors preserve Python's `self.freq` forwarding.
- Plugin boundary: `AccountBarMarket: Send + Sync` isolates suspension and last-valid-close access from account sequencing. `AccountPosition: Send + Sync` now includes stock enumeration, price mutation, and count mutation alongside the completed order-accounting operations. `ExchangeQuoteProvider` and the built-in finite/infinite positions implement these interfaces. The account owns ordering, short-circuit, and partial-mutation policy, preventing plugins from moving count increments ahead of price refresh. These are in-process traits; owned DTO versioning, discovery, and component/process transport remain future physical-plugin work.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono supplies timestamps, `thiserror` supplies typed plugin errors, Arrow-backed `ExchangeQuoteProvider` supplies quote conversion, and `indexmap` continues to preserve finite-position stock order. A new market-data crate would duplicate the completed quote stack; async/Tokio would change the synchronous upstream flow; a plugin registry or ABI crate is premature before stable owned DTOs exist.
