## Portfolio metrics storage and benchmark sampling

- Contract: Store the nine aligned portfolio columns under one ordered datetime key. Updating an existing timestamp replaces its row without moving its original insertion position, while `latest_pm_time` always follows the most recent update call even when that timestamp is older. All nine non-benchmark inputs are required. An explicit benchmark value bypasses end-time and provider access; otherwise end time is required, an absent benchmark source stores a missing value, and a configured source samples the closed interval. In-memory benchmark series are stably timestamp-sorted, include both bounds and duplicates, compound `(return + 1)` in row order, skip NaN like Pandas `prod`, return zero for a selected all-NaN interval, and return no value for an empty interval. Arrow export preserves Pandas column order. CSV load resets rows after header validation, accepts reordered/additional columns, loads iteratively, and retains rows preceding a later parse failure.
- In scope: Frequency and benchmark reinitialization; empty/latest access; all required update fields; explicit, absent, successful, empty, and failed benchmark sampling; insertion order, overwrite, and last-call semantics; finite values, NaN, and infinities; Arrow `RecordBatch` export with microsecond datetimes and nullable benchmark; path and generic `Read`/`Write` CSV persistence; reordered/extra/missing columns; date-only and fractional timestamps; null benchmark round-trip; I/O, CSV, datetime, numeric, short-row, and partial-load failures; and live AST execution of the authoritative Python record/update/DataFrame methods.
- Out of scope: Automatic CSI300 or instrument-list feature retrieval from Qlib's global data service, timezone-aware datetime preservation, Pandas' full permissive datetime parser, duplicate datetime rows in externally authored CSV, arbitrary Python object values in nominally numeric fields, account-value calculation, historical positions, risk analysis, indicator orchestration, PyO3 conversion, remote plugin transport, discovery, isolation, and a stable native ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: One `IndexMap<NaiveDateTime, PortfolioMetricRecord>` replaces nine separately aligned `OrderedDict` values, preventing cross-column drift while preserving insertion and overwrite behavior. `Option<f64>` represents an in-memory missing benchmark; CSV blank benchmark values load as NaN because Pandas `read_csv` likewise materializes the blank numeric cell as NaN before replaying updates. Arrow is the stable tabular boundary rather than exposing a DataFrame implementation. Required Python keyword arguments remain `Option` fields in `PortfolioMetricUpdate`, so missing-input failures remain observable. CSV and datetime parsing are deliberately typed; permissive Python object coercion remains a future Python binding concern.
- Plugin boundary: `BenchmarkReturnSampler: Send + Sync` isolates external benchmark lookup/sampling and supports in-memory, data-service, remote, or future component adapters. `BenchmarkReturnSeries` is the default local compatibility adapter. Generic CSV methods accept dynamic standard `Read`/`Write` boundaries, so files, memory, networks, and plugin streams reuse one parser without exposing the `csv` crate in the public contract. Record ordering, validation, table schema, and partial-load policy remain framework-owned domain behavior.
- Dependencies: Added workspace `csv 1.4.0` with default features disabled for maintained streaming CSV parsing/writing; metadata reports MSRV 1.73 (within the workspace's Rust 1.85) and MIT/Unlicense licensing. Existing third-party Arrow crates provide tabular interchange, Chrono provides timestamps, `indexmap` provides ordered overwrite semantics, and `thiserror` provides typed failures. Polars would add a large DataFrame runtime for a fixed nine-column table, handwritten CSV would violate the reuse policy and mishandle quoting/errors, and async I/O is unnecessary for the synchronous upstream class.

## Account portfolio-metric update

- Contract: An enabled finite account owns a portfolio ledger configured with the account frequency and optional benchmark sampler. The first row uses initial cash and zero cumulative cost/turnover as baselines; later rows use the ledger's latest updated row. Each update reads total account value, stock value, accumulated cost/turnover deltas, and immediately available cash in Python order, then stores return `(earning + incremental_cost) / previous_account`, cumulative and incremental turnover/cost rates, stock value, cash, and the benchmark sampled over the closed interval. A disabled or unsupported infinite position has no ledger. Valuation, cash, zero-baseline, and benchmark failures leave the ledger unchanged.
- In scope: Backward-compatible default/boxed/explicit-frequency constructors; optional benchmark-plugin construction; initial cash and ledger accessors; first and subsequent record baselines; cumulative-to-incremental cost/turnover calculation; available cash excluding delayed settlement; finite and infinite built-in position adapters; disabled metrics; total/stock/cash failures and their exact call boundaries; zero previous account value; benchmark failure atomicity; IEEE NaN/infinity preservation; and live AST execution of the authoritative Python method for two consecutive updates.
- Out of scope: Historical position deep copies, `now_account_value` storage, weight refresh, indicator update, complete `update_bar_end`, automatic data-service benchmark construction, timezone-aware timestamps, PyO3 compatibility, serialized external plugin DTOs, runtime discovery, process isolation, and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `AccountPosition` now exposes framework-owned valuation capabilities (`initial_cash`, `total_value`, `stock_value`, and `available_cash`) plus an explicit `portfolio_metrics_supported` capability. This avoids invoking side-effecting plugin methods during construction and lets infinite positions reject ledger creation deterministically. Python's disabled-ledger assertion and zero-division exception become typed `AccountError` variants; their mutation and evaluation boundaries remain equivalent. The account borrows its position and ledger as disjoint fields, so no cloning or hidden rollback is introduced. `PortfolioMetrics` remains the sole owner of benchmark sampling and ordered row mutation.
- Plugin boundary: Existing `AccountPosition: Send + Sync` is the replaceable valuation seam; built-in `Position` and `InfinitePosition` are adapters. Existing `BenchmarkReturnSampler: Send + Sync` remains independently replaceable and is accepted as `Arc<dyn BenchmarkReturnSampler>`. Framework code owns formula order, baselines, error atomicity, and ledger writes, preventing either plugin from redefining Qlib accounting semantics.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono supplies interval timestamps, `thiserror` supplies typed errors, `indexmap` underlies ordered records, and `Arc` provides shared benchmark-plugin ownership. A numeric/dataframe crate would not replace the small Qlib-specific accounting formula; async/Tokio would change the synchronous upstream contract; and a physical plugin ABI crate remains premature until owned, versioned DTOs are designed.

## Account historical-position snapshots

- Contract: `update_hist_positions` first calculates the current total account value, writes that value back to the current position as `now_account_value`, recalculates every stock's total-asset weight, deep-copies the fully refreshed position, and finally stores the independent copy under the bar start timestamp. Reusing a timestamp replaces its value without changing dictionary insertion order. A failure stops at its exact stage: prior current-position mutations remain, while history is untouched until snapshot creation succeeds.
- In scope: Optional stored account value on finite positions; account-value and stock-weight reads through the plugin interface; current-position account-value mutation; atomic built-in weight refresh; fallible owned snapshot creation; ordered historical storage and accessor; finite snapshot independence; stable timestamp overwrite; total-value, account-write, weight-refresh, and snapshot failures; built-in zero-value and infinite-position failures; and live AST execution of the original Python method across success and all four failure stages.
- Out of scope: Indicator reset/aggregation/recording, complete `update_bar_end`, automatic snapshot persistence, external wire serialization, timezone-aware timestamps, PyO3 dictionary conversion, runtime plugin discovery, process isolation, and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `Position` stores `Option<f64>` for Python's conditionally present `now_account_value`. `HistoricalPosition` owns a boxed position plugin plus the aligned account value, so snapshots are independent and remain inspectable through the stable `AccountPosition` interface. The account uses `IndexMap` to reproduce Python dictionary insertion and overwrite order. The Rust method is named `update_historical_positions` for clarity; the behavior and evaluation order match the Python method. Infinite positions fail at total-value calculation before any later mutation, as upstream does.
- Plugin boundary: `AccountPosition` now adds `stored_account_value`, `stock_weight`, `set_account_value`, `update_weights`, and fallible `history_snapshot`. The account owns orchestration and only inserts after all plugin stages succeed. A fallible snapshot operation supports in-process cloning today and future serialized or remote snapshots without forcing framework code to know plugin types. Built-in `Position` uses its existing deep `Clone`; `InfinitePosition` remains explicitly unsupported by the normal update path.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `indexmap` provides deterministic Python-compatible overwrite order, Chrono provides timestamp keys, and `thiserror` carries typed plugin failures. The `dyn-clone` crate was considered but rejected because its infallible clone contract cannot represent Python `deepcopy` failures or future remote serialization failures; the small Qlib-specific fallible snapshot method is therefore retained. Serde/Arrow are not needed until a physical persistence or interchange contract is selected.

## Account indicator orchestration

- Contract: `update_indicator` resets the indicator first. Atomic execution then consumes the current bar's trade executions; nested execution aggregates mutable inner order indicators using the outer decision, decision steps, market-data provider, and aggregation configuration. Both paths next calculate trade-level metrics for the bar start and account frequency, optionally emit the Python-compatible status line, and finally record the timestamped indicator snapshot. Every failure stops immediately and retains only mutations from earlier completed stages; output happens after calculation and before recording.
- In scope: Typed atomic and nested requests; forwarding of trade executions, inner stores, outer decisions, base-price steps/providers, aggregation configuration, calculation configuration, timestamp, frequency, and display flag; built-in `Indicator<NumpyOrderIndicator>` composition; reset, update/aggregate, calculate, display, and record ordering; current and recorded indicator access; replaceable indicator and output implementations; Python-compatible `nan`, `inf`, `-inf`, and integer-float display; every plugin failure boundary and partial state; real atomic/nested calculations; and live AST execution of the original Python method across success and every stage failure.
- Out of scope: Complete `update_bar_end` composition and its missing-input validation, executor ownership of inner indicators, timezone-aware timestamps, structured logging policy, serialized external plugin DTOs, runtime discovery, process isolation, and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `AccountIndicatorMode` makes Python's atomic branch explicit instead of accepting an ambiguous bag of optional parameters. `NestedAccountIndicatorUpdate` borrows and mutates inner stores exactly where upstream aggregation does. `show_indicator` is routed through an output seam after calculation, preserving Python's ordering while making tests and embedding deterministic. Rust uses typed errors instead of Python exceptions and does not roll back earlier indicator mutations. The formatter adds `.0` to finite integer-valued floats and uses lowercase special values to match Python's observable status line.
- Plugin boundary: `AccountIndicator: Send + Sync` is an object-safe in-process lifecycle seam for reset, atomic update, nested aggregation, calculation, and recording; the framework still owns their ordering. `AccountIndicatorOutput: Send + Sync` independently replaces stdout with logging, collection, or remote sinks without granting the sink control over indicator semantics. Both seams return dedicated typed errors. The built-in report indicator and stdout writer are default adapters, and `Account` supports replacement while returning the previous implementation.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono supplies timestamps, `indexmap` supplies deterministic metric ordering, and `thiserror` supplies typed plugin/output failures; the completed `Indicator`, `NumpyOrderIndicator`, decision, and base-price abstractions provide the domain implementation. A new numeric or logging crate would not replace this small Qlib-specific orchestration, and a dynamic-library/plugin-ABI crate remains premature until owned versioned DTOs and isolation requirements are defined.

## Synchronous nested-executor collection loop

- Contract: Initialize the inner executor over the current outer interval, attach its level infrastructure, and reset the inner strategy before checking completion. On every inner step, update the outer decision and call the strategy alteration hook only when the decision was replaced. A configured empty-decision short circuit exits after that update. Range resolution happens after decision update, falls back to the entire inner calendar when unavailable, and either advances an out-of-range step without strategy execution or generates an immediate inner decision. The outer decision modifies that decision, the interval is captured before inner collection advances the calendar, the post-step hook runs before flattening and snapshotting, and the just-completed result becomes the next strategy input. Normal exit finalizes the upper-level strategy once. The first failure stops without rollback.
- In scope: Outer interval initialization; inner reset and level binding; strategy reset; repeated completion checks; unchanged and replaced outer decisions; empty break enabled/disabled; explicit and missing ranges; aligned skips and alignment-disabled execution; immediate strategy decisions; outer-to-inner metadata propagation; pre-collection timestamps; recursive level increment; stable flattened result order; previous-result object identity; post-step and upper-level hooks; owned raw indicator snapshots; decision records and mutable indicator access for outer aggregation; every calendar/decision/strategy/executor/binding failure stage; owned conversion from atomic execution tuples; and live AST execution of the authoritative synchronous Python method.
- Out of scope: Python generator-returning strategies and caller-visible `yield from` pause/resume; concrete adapters for `TradeCalendarManager`, strategy implementations, `AtomicExecutorLifecycle`, and `Account`; nested `BaseExecutor.collect_data` settlement/bar-end/calendar wrapper; runtime discovery; cross-process transport; isolation; and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Python's flattened execution list and `_inner_execute_result` share the same contained objects. Rust represents each bottom-level execution as `Arc<OwnedOrderExecution>`, so both lists retain allocation identity without borrowing a mutable inner decision across later steps. `NestedDecisionRecord` owns each generated decision while storing the exact pre-collection calendar interval; it can materialize borrowed `BasePriceStep` values only while the collection lives. A mutable indicator-snapshot view is intentional because existing outer aggregation normalizes per-step trade prices in place. Decision replacement remains inside a stable `NestedOuterDecision` handle and is reported as `NestedDecisionUpdate::Replaced`, avoiding invalidating a trait-object reference while preserving the conditional strategy hook.
- Plugin boundary: `NestedCalendar`, `NestedOuterDecision`, `NestedStrategy`, `NestedInnerExecutor`, and `NestedLevelBinding` are independent process-local traits with dedicated typed diagnostics. `NestedExecutorCore` alone owns ordering, short circuits, range alignment, failure retention, result flattening, and snapshot timing, so a plugin cannot silently reorder Qlib's transaction semantics. The traits expose Qlib-owned DTOs rather than third-party executor types. Physical plugins still require owned versioned wire DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono carries closed timestamps and `thiserror` supplies typed plugin failures; existing Qlib-owned order, decision, base-price, and dense-indicator types are reused. Standard-library `Arc` preserves shared result identity. Tokio/futures were rejected because this path is synchronous and no scheduling or I/O concurrency is observable. Generator crates were not selected because stable Rust generators do not directly reproduce Python's bidirectional `yield from`; that control-transfer surface should be an explicit resumable state machine in its own characterized slice. `dyn-clone` would clone plugin objects rather than the owned domain values needed here.

## Nested base lifecycle and concrete account bridge

- Contract: The optional decision tracker runs first and models resumption after Python's outer `yield`. A non-`None` settlement begins before nested collection. After the synchronous inner loop returns, the outer calendar interval is read at that exact point, the real account receives nested mode with the current outer decision, mutable inner indicator snapshots, captured decision steps, calculation configuration, and aggregation configuration, then the outer calendar advances. Settlement commit follows calendar advancement, the optional return sink runs last, and the owned nested collection is returned unchanged. Every failure retains all previously reached state and suppresses later stages.
- In scope: Tracking enabled with and without a consumer; tracking disabled; settlement enabled/disabled; nested core success and failure conversion; the second outer-calendar timestamp read; real nested account bar-end forwarding; mutable indicator/decision-step pairing without copying decisions; outer calendar advancement; settlement commit; optional return storage; all lifecycle error domains and precise ordering; real finite and infinite account settlement behavior; real account indicator recording; account market-error conversion; and live AST execution of the nested path through authoritative `BaseExecutor.collect_data`.
- Out of scope: A concrete `NestedInnerExecutor` adapter over `AtomicExecutorLifecycle`; construction/reset of actual Qlib strategy objects; generator-producing RL strategy suspension and sent values; dynamic configuration discovery; Python/PyO3 bindings; serialization; cross-process transport; isolation; and stable native plugin ABI.

## Concrete atomic nested-inner adapter

- Contract: Reset the exact shared inner calendar to the outer bar before execution; expose its finished/length/current-step/current-interval/step operations to the nested loop; run each generated inner decision through the completed atomic base lifecycle and simulator collector; copy every borrowed atomic execution into an independently owned shared value before the decision can be released; and copy the completed inner account's raw order indicator after the atomic bar has updated it. The atomic lifecycle advances the same calendar observed by the nested loop, so one completed atomic step terminates a one-step inner window. The first reset, atomic lifecycle, account, collection, or snapshot failure is returned as a typed nested-inner diagnostic without rollback.
- In scope: Object-safe resettable calendar composition across `NestedCalendar`, `ExecutorLifecycleCalendar`, and `SimulatorCalendar`; real `AtomicExecutorLifecycle`; real `SimulatorCollector`; real `AtomicAccountAdapter` and inner `Account`; owned `Arc<OwnedOrderExecution>` conversion; inner indicator snapshots; success and reset/collection/snapshot failures; all calendar delegates; an end-to-end real `NestedExecutorLifecycle` updating a second real outer `Account`; and live composition of the authoritative Python `BaseExecutor.collect_data` and `NestedExecutor._collect_data` methods.
- Out of scope: A concrete Rust port of `TradeCalendarManager.reset`; construction from Qlib configuration dictionaries; concrete strategy and outer-decision adapters; Python generator-producing strategies and bidirectional `yield from`; PyO3 bindings; runtime plugin discovery; cross-process transport; isolation; and stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `AtomicNestedInnerAdapter` owns one `AtomicExecutorLifecycle` and borrows the mutable collector/account for the duration of a synchronous nested call. `NestedCalendar` requires `Send` rather than `Sync`, because an executor holding an exclusive account borrow cannot honestly be shared concurrently; the separately shared `ResettableNestedCalendar` remains `Sync` and also requires `ExecutorLifecycleCalendar`, making one object-safe calendar contract serve both lifecycle views. Borrowed simulator executions are copied immediately into `Arc`-owned domain values, preserving shared allocation identity between the previous-result strategy hook and flattened result while preventing later decision mutation from changing retained fills. The adapter always disables atomic tracking and return storage because those caller-visible boundaries belong to the enclosing nested lifecycle.
- Plugin boundary: `ResettableNestedCalendar` is an object-safe in-process composition seam; implementations own reset/index/time semantics while framework code owns sequencing. `AtomicExecutorAccount::order_indicator_snapshot` exposes one Qlib-owned dense DTO without downcasting account plugins. Strategy, binding, outer-decision, dealer, reporter, market, base-price, inner account, and outer account remain independently replaceable. Physical plugins still require versioned owned DTOs and a component/process protocol.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono supplies closed timestamps and `thiserror` supplies typed errors; existing Arrow-backed market/report boundaries and dense NumPy-compatible indicator storage are reused. Standard-library `Arc` is the correct zero-runtime shared-ownership primitive. Tokio/futures would add scheduling semantics absent from this synchronous contract, and `dyn-clone` would clone plugin objects instead of producing the required owned execution and dense-indicator DTOs.

## Explicit resumable nested/RL control transfer

- Contract: A newly created executor accepts only `Continue`. With outer tracking enabled, it yields an owned outer-decision snapshot before settlement or initialization side effects. Resumption begins settlement, resets and binds the inner executor, resets the strategy, then performs the existing update/alter/empty/range loop. A suspended strategy yields a versioned prompt and receives only the value sent at that prompt; values sent while resuming either tracked-decision yield are ignored, matching Python's bare `yield trade_decision`. Repeated strategy prompts remain suspended. A ready inner decision is modified and timestamped before its optional tracking yield, then collected on resumption. Completion preserves post-execute, snapshot, upper-level, outer bar, calendar step, settlement commit, and return-sink ordering. The first plugin failure unwinds the logical generator and all later resumes return the stable terminal failure state.
- In scope: Immediate and suspended strategies; initial protocol validation; outer and inner tracked decisions; repeated prompts; `Continue` and optional numeric actions; decision-yield action suppression; settlement enabled/disabled; empty skipping enabled/disabled; range alignment enabled/disabled; lower and upper out-of-range steps; replacement alteration; previous-result propagation; owned execution, decision, and prompt state across suspension; final account aggregation and return storage; every calendar, binding, decision, strategy, inner-executor, account, and sink failure boundary; error continuations after strategy resumption and after an inner tracking yield; terminal complete/failed behavior; Serde round trips; and live execution of the authoritative Python generator methods through AST extraction.
- Out of scope: Suspending a recursively nested child executor inside this one-level driver; concrete ports of `SAOEStrategy`, `ProxySAOEStrategy`, policies, interpreters, and Qlib configuration construction; Python/PyO3 bindings; process discovery; isolation; and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `ResumableNestedExecutor` is an explicit phase machine rather than an async task: the characterized Python code exposes bidirectional control transfer but no scheduling, I/O readiness, or concurrent wakeups. `NestedStrategyProgress` preserves the immediate fast path and adds an owned suspended prompt. `NestedExecutorResume` and `NestedStrategyPrompt` are Serde DTOs suitable for a future component boundary; prompts carry a kind, schema version, and opaque payload. `TrackedOrderDecision` owns its orders and interval so no mutable strategy or decision borrow escapes. `NestedDecisionTracking` groups independently selectable outer/inner yield policy without an excessive boolean configuration surface. Terminal protocol errors are distinguished from plugin errors so observing an already completed or failed machine does not mutate its terminal state.
- Plugin boundary: Strategy implementations provide `begin_trade_decision` and `resume_trade_decision` while the framework exclusively owns lifecycle ordering and the meaning of sent values. Calendar, binding, outer decision, inner executor, account, and return sink remain independent typed traits. A plugin cannot bypass settlement or account ordering, and all data retained across a suspension is Qlib-owned. The process-local trait surface is plugin-ready but not an ABI; physical plugins still require a versioned component/process transport and isolation policy.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party `serde` supplies the versioned resume/prompt wire representation, `thiserror` supplies typed terminal and plugin diagnostics, and Chrono supplies closed interval timestamps. Standard-library ownership and trait objects implement the state machine. Tokio, futures, coroutine crates, and generator emulation were rejected because they would introduce scheduling or unstable control semantics not present in the characterized source.

## Recursive child-session control propagation

- Contract: A recursively nested inner executor owns its generated outer decision for the complete child session and explicitly reports either a tracked decision, a strategy prompt, or an owned completion containing that same decision and its shared executions. The parent forwards child events without emitting a duplicate local inner-decision yield. When the simulator supplies an action, the strategy driver repeats that same action across every intermediate tracked-decision yield until it reaches the exact suspended child strategy, matching `_iter_strategy`; bare decision yields ignore the value. Child completion returns to the parent loop, which performs post-step, snapshot, outer aggregation, settlement, and calendar effects exactly once. A child begin or resume failure terminates the parent state machine.
- In scope: Framework-controlled synchronous collection and delegated recursive collection modes; default owned synchronous begin and invalid-resume behavior; owned decisions across suspension; typed tracked-decision and strategy-prompt propagation; recursive child begin/resume; exact action forwarding through multiple intermediate yields; decision inventory equivalent to the simulator's `decisions`; child completion; adapter delegation for reset, all five calendar methods, collection rejection outside the resumable protocol, and indicator snapshots; framework tracking followed by an independently suspended inner session; child begin/resume failure propagation; initial-action protocol failure; stable parent failure state; and live AST execution of two nested executors over one tracked atomic executor through the authoritative `_iter_strategy` method.
- Out of scope: Construction of a production child session from Qlib configuration; an owned factory that assembles `ResumableNestedExecutor` collaborators for arbitrary depth; concrete `SAOEStrategy`/`ProxySAOEStrategy`, order-helper, policy, interpreter, observation, reward, and simulator data ports; Python/PyO3 bindings; process discovery; isolation; and a stable native plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `NestedInnerControlMode::Framework` preserves the completed synchronous fast path, while `Delegated` makes the child session solely responsible for exposing its own outer tracking yield and prevents the parent from duplicating it. `NestedInnerProgress::Complete` returns both the originally owned decision and shared executions, so the parent can retain its decision record after arbitrary suspension without cloning a trait object. `RecursiveStrategyDriver` stores owned decision snapshots and applies one immutable resume input repeatedly inside its loop, reproducing the unusual Python behavior where the same sent action crosses non-strategy yields. The driver returns either the next prompt or final collection rather than treating generator exhaustion as an error.
- Plugin boundary: `NestedChildSession` is the narrow stateful plugin seam for beginning and resuming one owned child collection. `RecursiveNestedInnerAdapter` composes that seam with the already completed calendar/account lifecycle boundary and advertises delegated control explicitly. The framework owns routing, parent phase transitions, action repetition, terminal-state semantics, and result recording; child plugins cannot cause parent settlement or bar effects to be applied twice. All cross-suspension values are Qlib-owned DTOs, but the traits remain process-local and are not a stable ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono provides owned interval timestamps, Serde continues to provide resume/prompt wire DTOs, and `thiserror` carries typed nested errors. Standard-library ownership and trait objects are sufficient for recursive control transfer. Tokio, futures, async recursion, and coroutine crates were rejected because the source exposes synchronous generator delegation rather than scheduling or I/O readiness.

## Concrete SAOE state and proxy strategy boundary

- Contract: `SAOEState` retains the exact Python named-tuple field order and owns the sole outer order, current time and step, remaining position, execution and step histories, optional scalar/vector metrics, backtest features, tick indices, and ticks-per-step. Reset accepts exactly one dated outer order. Beginning a decision reads and stores the current step range before yielding a versioned proxy locator. Resuming forwards the optional numeric action to the order helper before reading the step interval and returning one child order. Post-step handling is a no-op for a zero-length range with no executions, rejects executions for that range, groups positive-range fills by order/day, updates the adapter even for an empty matching group, and finalizes only at the upper-level hook.
- In scope: Owned `SaoeState`, `SaoeStateParts`, `SaoeBacktestData`, `SaoeMetrics`, scalar/ndarray numeric and scalar/vector timestamp variants; Bincode state envelope; Arrow IPC history/feature batches; exact preservation of `NaN`; versioned JSON prompt locators; resumable proxy phases; outer-order validation; action/order-helper ordering; closed step times; same-day execution grouping; state access before and during suspension; zero-range semantics; every calendar, state, order-factory, Arrow, Bincode, JSON, order-time, and protocol failure boundary; and direct AST execution of the authoritative Python state and strategy classes.
- Out of scope: The calculations inside Python `SAOEStateAdapter.update`, feature acquisition and resampling, final metric formulas, policy/interpreter/observation/reward implementations, `SingleAssetOrderExecution` simulator assembly, configured recursive child-session construction, Python/PyO3 bindings, runtime plugin discovery, process isolation, and a stable native ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `SaoeNumeric` explicitly distinguishes a scalar from an owned `ndarray::Array1`, avoiding lossy coercion and preserving IEEE values. Tabular histories and features remain Arrow `RecordBatch` values instead of bespoke row structs. The state wire format serializes fixed metadata with Bincode and embeds each table as an Arrow IPC stream; this preserves schema and null semantics and avoids JSON's inability to represent `NaN`. `ProxySaoeStrategy` uses an explicit uninitialized/ready/suspended phase enum so illegal resume and duplicate begin operations are typed failures and the last observed range cannot diverge from the retained order. The yielded Python object becomes a versioned owned locator containing stock, normalized day, direction, and step range.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeCalendar`, `SaoeStateProvider`, and `SaoeOrderFactory` are narrow object-safe in-process traits. Framework code owns phase transitions, prompt schema validation, grouping, and lifecycle order; plugins supply calendar data, state materialization/update/finalization, and exchange-specific child-order construction. All suspension and state payloads are owned and serializable, but the traits are intentionally not presented as a stable binary ABI.
- Dependencies: Added mature third-party `arrow-ipc` 59.2 for schema-preserving state tables and `bincode` 1.3 for the compact owned envelope. Enabled existing Chrono and ndarray Serde support. Existing `serde_json` encodes the small interoperable prompt locator, `thiserror` provides typed diagnostics, Arrow supplies `RecordBatch`, and `Arc` preserves shared execution identity. No custom array, table, or binary codec was introduced.

## Concrete SAOE state calculations

- Contract: Construction records the initial calendar step, computes a NaN-skipping TWAP baseline, starts with empty metric histories, and positions current time at the later of the first order tick and order start. Each inclusive update maps child executions onto the CN sampled-minute index, keeps only the latest fill per minute, linearly scales a positive overfill to the remaining position, reports only material overfill greater than `position + 1`, obtains vector market price and volume, fills NaNs with the vector `nanmedian`, records per-tick metrics using the executor's latest PA, records one aggregate step metric, then subtracts position and advances to the next aligned step or order end. Finalization aggregates the full execution history and intentionally preserves upstream's second subtraction in the final `position` metric.
- In scope: Constructor validation; reset/reuse; current time and step; exact sampled CN minute indexing, including pre-session partition behavior; missing execution interval failures; upper and lower out-of-step fills; duplicate/current-time failures; overfill warning threshold and scaling; market and executor-context plugin ordering; odd/even/all-NaN median fill; scalar trade price/value/FFR/PA calculations for buy, sell, zero baseline, no fill, NaN, and infinities; per-tick and per-step ordered histories; final metrics; Arrow `RecordBatch` schemas and nanosecond timestamp validation; state Bincode/Arrow round trip; partial mutations when the final time advance fails; and direct AST execution of the original Python adapter and utility functions.
- Out of scope: Loading `IntradayBacktestData` from feature storage, choosing exchange expressions, constructing the executor/account/calendar graph, policies, action/state interpreters, observation and reward implementations, the `SingleAssetOrderExecution` simulator wrapper, Python/PyO3 bindings, external plugin discovery, process isolation, and a stable native ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Mutable initialization is represented by one optional session containing the order, current time, and validated end time, preventing impossible half-initialized states. Metric histories are accumulated as typed scalar rows and materialized as Arrow only at the owned state boundary. Market vectors use owned ndarray arrays. The exact Python arithmetic order is retained: `NaN * 0` remains `NaN`, a near overfill is silently scaled, a zero execution sum selects trade price zero, ordinary means do not skip remaining NaNs, and final position is calculated from the already-reduced adapter position. CN sampled minutes reuse the completed Qlib calendar implementation instead of a second clock table.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeAdapterMarket` supplies only a closed-interval price/volume vector. `SaoeAdapterContext` supplies current trade step, latest executor PA, and the overfill warning sink. `ConcreteSaoeStateAdapter` owns every calculation and implements the previously frozen `SaoeStateProvider` trait, so `ProxySaoeStrategy` can use it without knowing the exchange or executor implementation. Plugin failures are converted to the stable SAOE diagnostic at that trait boundary while direct callers retain typed `SaoeAdapterError` variants.
- Dependencies: Reused the existing mature Arrow 59.2 arrays/schema and IPC stack, ndarray 0.17 owned vectors, Chrono timestamps/durations, `num-traits` checked numeric conversions, and `thiserror`. No new dependency or custom table/array/serialization framework was introduced.

## Owned configured child-session assembly

- Contract: Every child `begin` asks a factory to construct a fresh, fully owned nested executor graph from the incoming outer decision and recursion level. The session retains the original decision and exact executor phase across tracked-decision and strategy-prompt suspensions, routes each resume input to that graph, and returns the original decision with the completed shared executions. A second begin is rejected while active; resume is rejected while idle; completion releases the graph so the same session can assemble the next child. Construction and executor failures remain typed child errors, while a failed executor preserves its terminal state.
- In scope: Owned calendar, level binding, inner executor, strategy, outer decision, account, and optional return-sink collaborators; removal of executor and recursive-adapter borrow lifetimes; per-decision factory assembly; level propagation; idle/active protocol validation; outer and inner tracking propagation; SAOE prompt/action routing; owned completion; graph disposal and reuse; construction failure; executor failure and failed continuation; compatibility with the existing recursive driver; and the authoritative multi-level Python differential already exercised by that driver.
- Out of scope: Parsing Python/YAML Qlib configuration, feature loading, concrete exchange/account/calendar builders, policy and action/state interpreters, observation and reward implementations, `SingleAssetOrderExecution` result packaging, Python/PyO3 bindings, external plugin discovery, process isolation, and a stable native ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `ResumableNestedExecutor` now owns its collaborators instead of borrowing them, eliminating the self-referential structure that would otherwise be required to retain a configured child graph across a prompt. Its calendar is an owned `Box<dyn NestedCalendar>` rather than `Arc<dyn NestedCalendar>` because the existing contract correctly requires `Send` but not `Sync`; this lets stateful calendars remain single-owner plugins. `NestedChildAssemblyFactory` observes but cannot retain a decision borrow. `ConfiguredNestedChildSession` separately retains the original boxed decision, allowing the factory to build an independent outer-decision adapter and allowing the parent to receive the exact original object at completion.
- Plugin boundary: `NestedChildAssemblyFactory` is the construction seam for configuration-aware child graphs. `ResumableNestedRun` is an owned bundle of independently replaceable process-local plugins, and `ConfiguredNestedChildSession` exclusively owns lifecycle and resume routing. Concrete SAOE construction can now supply `ProxySaoeStrategy` with its owned calendar, `ConcreteSaoeStateAdapter`, and order factory without unsafe code, leaked objects, or self references. These traits are plugin-ready composition boundaries, not a stable binary ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Chrono, Serde, `thiserror`, Arrow, ndarray, and Bincode remain the appropriate domain and wire-format libraries. Standard-library `Box`, `Arc`, and trait objects provide the required exclusive and shared ownership. Self-referential, async, coroutine, and dependency-injection crates were not needed because the graph is rebuilt synchronously at a well-defined factory boundary.

## Basic SAOE policy and interpreter boundary

- Contract: State interpreters convert one owned `SaoeState` snapshot into a serializable policy observation. The dummy interpreter emits the integer sentinel `1`; the current-step interpreter preserves direction, step, episode length, target amount, and remaining position while rejecting an impossible episode bound. Action interpreters validate the policy action type and range before reproducing Qlib's categorical grid/final-step liquidation or remaining-day TWAP-relative volume. Policies return one owned scalar action per observation; `AllOnePolicy` fills the batch with its configured scalar and preserves discrete versus continuous type.
- In scope: Versioned Serde observation/action/action-space DTOs; object-safe state interpreter, action interpreter, and batched policy traits; dummy and current-step observations; generated and explicit categorical actions; optional final-step liquidation; position and order-amount clipping; continuous non-negative validation; ceiling-based TWAP step estimation; zero tick stride and zero remaining-step failures; negative remaining-step arithmetic; empty and non-empty AllOne batches; discrete and continuous fill values; JSON round trips; and direct AST execution of the authoritative Python interpreter and policy classes.
- Out of scope: Full-history processed features and masking, Gym object replication, Tianshou batches, PPO/DQN inference and training, Torch checkpoint loading, recurrent/attention networks, rewards, strategy batching, concrete configuration parsing, and external plugin transport.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust represents Gym spaces as small serializable `SaoeActionSpace` DTOs instead of introducing a partial Gym clone. `SaoePolicyAction` keeps discrete and continuous values distinct, preventing the implicit NumPy dtype coercion from leaking across plugin boundaries. Python assertions and Gym validation become typed `SaoeInterpreterError` values. Floating conversion from integer counts is intentionally explicit because Python performs the same potentially inexact conversion. Negative remaining TWAP steps retain Python arithmetic; only the exact zero denominator is rejected.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeStateInterpreter`, `SaoeActionInterpreter`, and `SaoePolicy` are independent object-safe process-local seams. A configured strategy can combine a baseline or learned policy with any compatible state/action pair while the framework owns batching and count validation. Owned Serde DTOs are suitable for a later component/process protocol, but the Rust traits are not a stable ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Serde supplies the owned wire DTOs, `thiserror` supplies diagnostics, and the already migrated `SaoeState` retains Arrow/ndarray data. A Rust Gym or ML runtime was not added for the baseline slice; those dependencies should be selected only with the concrete PPO/DQN/network compatibility requirements in hand.

## Full-history SAOE observation processing

- Contract: The processed-data provider receives stock, order date, feature width, and the state's complete tick index and returns owned today/yesterday float32 matrices plus today's timestamps. Both matrices must match `(data_ticks, data_dim)`. Today's rows at or after the current time are zeroed inclusively; yesterday is retained. Position history starts with the outer order amount, appends every step position from Arrow Float32/Float64 history, fills with zero, and exposes exactly `max_step` values. Current tick counts state ticks strictly before current time and clips to the final observation row; current step clips to `max_step - 1`. Scalar observation fields reproduce NumPy int32/float32 conversion.
- In scope: Owned ndarray processed data; object-safe provider calls and failures; fixed dimension validation; provider argument fidelity; today/yesterday and index shape checks; inclusive masking; buy/sell acquisition flag; clipped and unclipped tick/step paths; Float32 and Float64 Arrow position history; missing, wrong-type, null, and overlong history failures; missing order start time; float32/int32 DTO serialization; and direct AST execution of the authoritative Python full-history interpreter.
- Out of scope: Concrete processed feature storage, feature expression calculation, cache policy, observation normalization beyond upstream canonicalization, Gym runtime objects, recurrent/attention networks, learned policies, rewards, and strategy batching.
- Compatibility decisions: Arrow remains the state/history interchange format and ndarray remains the dense observation representation. The provider boundary returns f32 matrices because Python canonicalizes the complete observation before policy invocation. Null Arrow positions are rejected rather than silently reading validity-buffer placeholders; the concrete Python-produced history never contains nulls. Dimension values are constrained to positive int32-compatible sizes because those fields are explicitly NumPy int32 and Gym shapes cannot represent a useful zero-sized episode here. `ndarray::s!` was avoided because its macro-level lint allowance conflicts with the workspace's command-line `unsafe_code = forbid`; a safe iterator creates the fixed history prefix instead.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeProcessedDataProvider` owns feature lookup and storage concerns. `FullHistoryStateInterpreter` owns Qlib masking, dtype, shape, clipping, and history semantics, so storage plugins cannot vary the policy observation contract. The provider uses owned ndarray data and Qlib timestamps rather than leaking a DataFrame implementation across the boundary.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party Arrow supplies typed history columns, ndarray supplies fixed dense matrices/vectors and Serde support, Chrono supplies dates/timestamps, Serde supplies observation transport, and `thiserror` supplies typed failures. A DataFrame crate was unnecessary because the characterized operation is a fixed-shape matrix mask and one typed Arrow column.

## SAOE policy batch pipeline

- Contract: A decision batch preserves input state order while interpreting every state, invokes the policy exactly once with the complete observation batch, requires exactly one action per state, then interprets state/action pairs in the same order into execution volumes. Empty input produces one empty policy batch and an empty volume list. The first state, policy, output-count, or action failure stops the pipeline.
- In scope: Owned state/interpreter/policy/action collaborators; stable batch ordering; empty batches; mixed state direction/position; exact policy output-count validation; state, policy, shape, and action failure propagation; compatibility with categorical and AllOne components; and live Python zip/batch output comparison.
- Out of scope: Order creation/filtering, trade-details rows, calendar/frequency metadata, outer-decision adapters, concrete `NestedStrategy` implementation, Torch/Tianshou integration, and learned inference.
- Compatibility decisions: `SaoePolicyPipeline` owns boxed object-safe plugins so it can be placed directly inside a configured strategy graph. Policy batching is explicit rather than emulating Tianshou `Batch`; the stable owned observation vector is the actual semantic boundary. Unlike Python's silent `zip` truncation, an action-count mismatch is a typed failure, preventing unexecuted outer orders from disappearing at a plugin boundary.
- Plugin boundary: State, policy, and action components remain independently replaceable. The pipeline owns sequencing and cardinality, while plugins own only their transformation or inference operation. All retained cross-boundary values are Serde-capable Qlib DTOs.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Vec/iterator primitives implement stable batching; Serde/ndarray/Arrow remain the observation representations. Adding Tianshou or an ML runtime would not improve this domain orchestration and is deferred to the concrete learned-policy slice.

## Immediate SAOE decision assembly

- Contract: `SaoeIntDecisionBuilder` snapshots one state per outer order in stable order, runs one complete policy/interpreter batch, creates child orders only when the interpreted volume is unequal to zero, then emits one detail row for every outer order. Detail rows retain instrument, current step start, frequency, execution volume, and the typed policy action. After details are complete, the builder reads the calendar once more to initialize the concrete order decision interval, matching Python argument evaluation and `TradeDecisionWO` construction order.

Rust rejects policy cardinality mismatches before assembly as previously documented. The typed policy contract cannot currently emit Python `None`; consequently every accepted decision detail contains `Some(action)`. The detail DTO keeps the action optional so a later dynamically typed or wire policy adapter can preserve Python's omitted `rl_action` column semantics without changing the report shape. Calendar calls deliberately occur once per detail row and once during decision construction because failures and mutable calendar plugins make those reads observable upstream.

The builder alone owns batch cardinality, stable pairing, filtering, report shape, and call order. `SaoeTradeDetail`, `SaoePolicyAction`, and the related observation/decision DTOs use owned Serde-compatible values; trait objects remain an internal Rust boundary rather than a stable ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Chrono supplies decision timestamps, Serde supplies detail/action transport, and `thiserror` supplies typed stage diagnostics. ## Lifecycle-owning immediate SAOE strategy

- Contract: `SaoeIntStrategy` resets an ordered adapter registry from the outer decision and clears its last range. Before every immediate decision it obtains the available inclusive data-calendar range and retains it, then delegates state batching, policy/action interpretation, child-order filtering, and detail construction to `SaoeIntDecisionBuilder`. After execution, a positive-length range groups all results by owned stock/day/direction key before updating each registered adapter in stable order, including empty groups. A zero-length range accepts only an empty result. Upper-level completion finalizes every adapter in stable order.
- In scope: Concrete `NestedStrategy` implementation; reset/generate/post-execute/post-upper-level lifecycle; missing-reset diagnostics; available-range failure and mutation order; ordered adapter construction; duplicate-key replacement without order movement; outer-decision metadata at adapter creation; state lookup; owned execution grouping; ignored unknown execution keys; empty adapter updates; key conversion failures before mutation; zero-range invariant; sequential partial update/finalize failures; no-op outer-decision alteration matching the upstream default; and direct AST execution of the authoritative Python lifecycle methods.
- Out of scope: Concrete `SaoeStateAdapterFactory` backed by market/data infrastructure, parsing Qlib configuration dictionaries, wiring the immediate strategy into `NestedChildAssemblyFactory`, reward calculation, PPO/DQN/network inference, Torch checkpoint compatibility, Python bindings, and physical plugin isolation.
- Compatibility decisions: The registry uses an owned `(String, NaiveDateTime, OrderDir)` key equivalent to Python `Order.key_by_day`. Existing-key insertion replaces the adapter while retaining its first insertion position, matching ordered Python dictionaries. All execution keys are validated and grouped before any adapter update, preserving Python's `defaultdict` construction-before-update failure boundary. Adapters are created before the outer order key is materialized because Python evaluates the assignment right-hand side before its subscript target. `alter_outer_decision` intentionally remains a no-op because upstream `SAOEStrategy` inherits the base method and does not rebuild `adapter_dict` there.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeStateAdapterFactory` owns per-order data loading and concrete adapter construction. `SaoeAdapterRegistry` owns ordered identity, replacement, grouping, lookup, and lifecycle fan-out. `SaoeIntStateProvider` remains the replaceable aggregate lifecycle seam consumed by the builder, and `SaoeDecisionCalendar` extends the existing SAOE calendar contract with frequency metadata. All interfaces remain process-local Rust traits; no unstable third-party container type crosses the public boundary.
- Dependencies: No new dependency was added. Existing third-party `indexmap` implements ordered dictionary replacement and lookup semantics, Chrono and the Qlib order DTO provide owned keys, and `thiserror` retains typed stage diagnostics. A custom ordered map, DataFrame, async runtime, or dynamic loading crate would add no capability required by this slice.

## Cached SAOE intraday backtest data

- Contract: Cache successful loads by Python's stock/day/subsecond/direction key with capacity 100. On a miss, read exchange quote timestamps in source order, retain timestamps inside the closed order interval, require a time-based range, retain every tick whose time of day lies inside the closed range, then query deal prices before market volumes using the first and last retained values. Duplicate and non-monotonic timestamps remain unchanged. Failed loads are never cached.
- In scope: `get_ticks_slice`, `IntradayBacktestData` eager price/volume fields, and `load_backtest_data`; closed order and clock filtering; source ordering and duplicates; non-monotonic first/last query bounds; exact order-day cache key including retained subsecond precision; cache hits that ignore later order interval/range/source inputs; 100-entry LRU eviction; empty slices; missing order bounds; unsupported ranges; all three source failures; Arrow empty feature schema; state wire round-trip of price/volume arrays; and legacy state payload decoding.
- Out of scope: A concrete Exchange/Arrow quote source, executor calendar frequency and start-step calculation, the final `SaoeAdapterInputsProvider` composition, processed feature loading, cross-process cache sharing, rewards, learned policies, network/checkpoint compatibility, Python bindings, and external plugin loading.
- Compatibility decisions: Pandas `DatetimeIndex.slice_indexer(datetime.time, datetime.time)` behaves as a stable time-of-day filter even for duplicate, non-monotonic, and multi-day input; Rust reproduces that behavior without sorting or deduplication. Python's unsupported-range path eventually raises `TypeError` and its empty time slice raises `IndexError` inside `IntradayBacktestData`; Rust exposes explicit `UnsupportedTradeRange` and `EmptyTradeRange` errors instead of reproducing accidental container failures. Cache entries are cloned into owned Rust state rather than returning mutable object identity, while cache-hit data and skipped source calls match Python. The cache is scoped to one loader/source rather than being process-global, preventing unrelated exchanges from sharing mutable cached objects. The expanded Bincode wire first attempts the new price/volume form and falls back to the prior payload shape with empty new arrays.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeBacktestDataSource` owns quote enumeration and direction-sensitive deal-price/volume access. `SaoeBacktestDataLoader` owns Qlib filtering, call order, cache key/capacity, empty handling, and the Arrow/ndarray state DTO. `TradeRange::time_bounds` is a defaulted object-safe capability; `TradeRangeByTime` opts in while index/custom ranges remain unsupported unless they explicitly provide clock bounds.
- Dependencies: Existing third-party `lru` supplies the bounded least-recently-used cache, Chrono supplies timestamp/date/time semantics, ndarray supplies owned numeric vectors, Arrow supplies the feature schema/record batch, Bincode supplies state transport, and `thiserror` supplies typed failures. No dependency was added. A custom cache or DataFrame implementation was rejected because `lru` and Arrow already provide the required general-purpose behavior.

## SAOE execution rewards

- Contract: `PAPenaltyReward` validates a positive target amount, reads the latest step row, selects execution rows at or after that step timestamp, computes price advantage times executed fraction plus the quadratic amount penalty, rejects a non-finite unscaled result, logs `reward/pa` before `reward/penalty`, and applies `scale` only after logging. `PPOReward` emits zero before termination, terminates at `cur_step + 1 == max_step` or remaining position below `1e-6`, uses an unweighted execution-price mean when total deal amount is exactly zero and a deal-amount-weighted mean otherwise, computes the direction-specific TWAP ratio with Python's zero-denominator fallbacks, and maps ratios with exact `< 1.0` and `< 1.1` boundaries.
- In scope: Both concrete rewards and defaults; object-safe reward and logging traits; Arrow history extraction; inclusive timestamp slicing; empty vectors; weighted and unweighted VWAP; buy/sell direction; zero denominators; threshold edges; Python-compatible NaN fall-through; invalid target amounts; missing, mistyped, null, and non-finite values; absent and failing loggers; scale ordering; stored PPO time-index configuration; and a live AST differential against the authoritative Python source.
- Out of scope: Generic `RewardCombination`, environment/logger attachment, configuration factories, trainer/environment orchestration, learned policy inference, Python bindings, and a stable native or sandboxed plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust returns typed `SaoeRewardError` variants instead of Python's incidental `AssertionError`, `KeyError`, `IndexError`, and Pandas dtype failures. A logger remains optional while constructing a reward, but calling the PA reward without one returns `MissingLogger`, matching the Python base-class assertion at use time. The Python finite check occurs before scale, so an infinite scaled return is intentionally preserved. PPO's NaN comparisons fall through to positive reward and are preserved. `start_time_index` and `end_time_index` are retained as configuration although the Python reward currently does not consume them. Canonical Arrow histories require nanosecond timestamps and `Float64` numeric columns.
- Plugin boundary: `SaoeReward` is an object-safe, process-local reward plugin over the stable `SaoeState` DTO. `SaoeRewardLogSink` is an independently replaceable logging plugin with its own typed failure domain. These are composition seams, not a stable binary ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing Apache Arrow crates provide typed columnar histories, `num-traits` provides checked numeric conversion used by the surrounding SAOE stack, and `thiserror` provides typed diagnostics. The reward formulas are Qlib-specific and small; a DataFrame, numerical framework, dependency-injection container, or dynamic-loading crate would add no required capability.

## Ordered reward composition

- Contract: Consume the supplied reward dictionary in insertion order. For each entry, call the child reward, multiply by its weight, add the weighted value to the running IEEE `f64` total, then log that weighted value under the dictionary key. Stop immediately at a child or logger failure while retaining all earlier child calls and log side effects. An empty combination returns `0.0` without requiring a logger. Environment attachment applies only to the top-level combination and is intentionally not propagated to children, matching Python's `EnvWrapper` assignment behavior.
- In scope: `RewardCombination`; object-safe heterogeneous children; unique named entries with stable Python-dict insertion/replacement order; positive, negative, zero, infinite, and NaN arithmetic; weighted log values including signed zero; empty input; late logger attachment and detachment; missing logger; child failure; logger failure after its side effect; non-recursive child logger lifecycle; and a live AST differential against `qlib.rl.reward`.
- Out of scope: Generic state types beyond the migrated `SaoeState`, configuration parsing and the currently disabled Python `reward_factory`, recursive child logger attachment, environment reset/step orchestration, reward-history storage, trainer copying/serialization, Python bindings, and a stable native or sandboxed plugin ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust child failures remain their original typed `SaoeRewardError` rather than being wrapped with the dictionary name, preserving Python's direct exception propagation. `MissingCombinationLogger` replaces the Python base-class assertion with an explicit error. Logger lookup happens after each child calculation and accumulation rather than before the loop; this is required for the Python-compatible empty case and partial state before a missing-logger failure. Inserting a duplicate key replaces its value without moving its original position, matching Python dictionaries. Child rewards are held in `Arc` for object-safe shared ownership; Python trainer `deepcopy` behavior remains a later orchestration concern.
- Plugin boundary: `RewardCombination` composes any process-local `SaoeReward` trait object and sends its own named weighted metrics through any `SaoeRewardLogSink`. The combination fixes Qlib ordering and failure semantics while leaving computation and logging transports replaceable.
- Dependencies: Existing third-party `indexmap` supplies deterministic unique-key insertion order and Python-compatible replacement position. Existing `thiserror` and standard `Arc` continue to supply typed diagnostics and shared plugin ownership. No dependency was added; a custom ordered map, dependency-injection framework, or dynamic plugin loader was rejected because it would duplicate `indexmap` or add behavior outside this slice.

## RL environment reset and finite-seed lifecycle

- Contract: A missing seed iterator means an indefinitely reusable unseeded factory, while an exhausted iterator is a permanent dead state. Every live reset clears logs before consuming a seed, calls the simulator factory with zero or one logical seed, replaces status before initial state/observation plugins execute, appends only a successfully interpreted initial observation, and returns an invalid observation when `StopIteration` arises anywhere in that reset chain. Later reset and step calls reject the dead environment. Ordinary plugin failures propagate without incorrectly marking the environment dead and retain the exact partial status reached by Python.
- In scope: Unseeded, seeded, and exhausted lifecycle states; repeated resets; object-safe simulator factory and observation-space plugins; uninitialized step runners; atomic simulator/status episode storage; logger binding for every optional component; initial observation history; typed dead/not-reset errors; explicit `StopIteration` plugin signaling; invalid-observation failures; factory/state/interpreter partial mutations; step delegation after reset; and a live AST extraction of `EnvWrapper.reset`.
- Out of scope: A concrete recursive Rust representation of NumPy/Gym samples, `fill_invalid`, `is_invalid`, Gym action/observation validation, `FiniteVectorEnv`, worker transports, trainer construction/copying, Python bindings, plugin discovery, and a stable binary ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust models Python's `SEED_INTERATOR_MISSING` sentinel as `EnvironmentSeedSource::Unseeded` and Python `None` exhaustion as `EnvironmentSeedSource::Exhausted`. The simulator and status live in one optional episode so impossible half-initialized combinations cannot exist, while a state/interpreter failure still retains the newly installed empty status. `EnvironmentPluginError::stop_iteration` is intentionally distinct from ordinary plugin failure because Python catches only that control-flow exception. `EnvironmentObservationSpace` owns invalid-observation generation so ndarray, tensor, structured-map, or foreign Gym adapters can preserve their native dtype and shape instead of narrowing the environment to one Rust tensor type.
- Plugin boundary: `EnvironmentSimulatorFactory` constructs any process-local simulator from an optional borrowed seed; `EnvironmentObservationSpace` supplies the exhausted sentinel in its native observation type; the existing simulator, state interpreter, action interpreter, reward, and auxiliary traits remain independently replaceable. These seams support static Rust plugins and adapters but are not a stable dynamic-library ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party `thiserror` supplies typed lifecycle diagnostics, `num-bigint` preserves Python step counters, and the existing `indexmap`/Serde stack remains in the composed step runner. Rust's standard `Iterator` exactly models finite seed consumption. A Gym clone or generic tensor dependency would not implement Qlib's sample-and-recursive-dtype invalidation by itself, so that behavior remains behind `EnvironmentObservationSpace` until the concrete `finite_env` value model is migrated.

## Finite-environment invalid observation values

- Contract: Convert every supported observation leaf to a new array of the same shape and dtype, using NaN for `float16`, `float32`, and `float64`, and the dtype maximum for signed/unsigned 8/16/32/64-bit integers. Recurse through ordered mappings, lists, and tuples without changing container order or kind. Checking is universal over every leaf, so empty arrays/containers are invalid and a first valid leaf short-circuits before a later malformed dtype. Bool and unsupported array dtypes reproduce NumPy `iinfo` failure, opaque objects fail filling but are considered invalid by Qlib's permissive final predicate branch. Observation generation samples first and then fills recursively.
- In scope: Eleven NumPy-compatible numeric dtypes; multidimensional and zero-dimensional ndarray values; nested map/list/tuple observations; stable map order; empty arrays and containers; all-valid, partially valid, short-circuit, and nested-error paths; bool, complex/unsupported-array, and opaque-object behavior; public check alias; sampling failures; conversion failures; and a concrete adapter to `EnvironmentObservationSpace<FiniteObservation>`.
- Out of scope: Complex, datetime, string, object, and structured arrays as valid fillable values; arbitrary non-string Python dictionary keys; ndarray stride/order metadata; random Gym space sampling implementations; stacked vector batches; worker transports; `FiniteVectorEnv`; trainer integration; and Python bindings.
- Compatibility decisions: Python/NumPy scalar inputs become zero-dimensional arrays during `fill_invalid`; Rust represents that canonical post-conversion form directly as `ArrayD` with rank zero. `FiniteObservation::UnsupportedArray` distinguishes dtype-bearing values that make NumPy `iinfo` fail from `Opaque`, which Qlib's `is_invalid` treats as true. The predicate returns `Result<bool, FiniteObservationError>` because Python can raise while checking bool or unsupported ndarray dtypes. `IndexMap` preserves Python dictionary order. The sampled-space adapter maps compatibility errors into the existing environment plugin failure domain without erasing their messages.
- Plugin boundary: `SampledFiniteObservationSpace` accepts any `Send` sampling closure, then owns Qlib's invalid conversion. Gym, Python, simulator-native, replay, or deterministic test samplers can therefore plug into reset without exposing their space implementation. `FiniteObservation` is the process-local recursive value boundary; it is not yet a stable cross-process or binary-plugin wire format.
- Dependencies: Existing third-party `ndarray` provides owned dynamic-dimensional numeric arrays, `half` supplies IEEE float16 and NaN behavior, `indexmap` supplies deterministic map order, and `thiserror` supplies typed compatibility failures. No dependency was added. A custom dense-array implementation was rejected in favor of `ndarray`; Arrow alone was rejected because it does not preserve arbitrary multidimensional observation shape, and a full Gym clone was rejected because sampling is already replaceable and would add unrelated space-validation behavior.

## Finite vector environment coordinator

- Contract: Initialize every backend worker as alive; warn on unguarded reset; validate and preserve requested worker order and duplicate IDs while sending only alive workers to the backend; retain Python's last-duplicate output/action slot and `zip` truncation behavior; retire a worker only when reset returns a missing or invalid observation; replace invalid step observations without retiring the worker; invoke reset loggers with the complete raw observation batch and step loggers before placeholder filling; capture the first observation, reward, and info defaults and clone them into missing output slots; transition permanently to zombie state when no worker remains; and guard collection with ordered ready/done callbacks while converting only exhaustion into a normal empty result.
- In scope: Transport-neutral batched reset and step coordination; deterministic alive-worker ordering; explicit worker selection; duplicate/remapping behavior; reset retirement and zombie lifecycle; persistent deep-cloned defaults; logger ordering and callback arguments; guarded and unguarded collection; normal, exhaustion, backend, predicate, logger, selection, and action-length failures; a concrete recursive predicate for `FiniteObservation`; and live AST execution of the authoritative Python class methods.
- Out of scope: Tianshou `DummyVectorEnv`, `SubprocVectorEnv`, and `ShmemVectorEnv` process/shared-memory implementations; `vectorize_env` construction and environment-factory serialization; NumPy stacked return arrays; Gym action/observation spaces; `LogWriter` aggregation internals; trainer integration; Python bindings; runtime plugin discovery; and a stable dynamic-library ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `IndexSet<usize>` preserves Python set-like membership with deterministic worker iteration. Requested IDs remain a vector so duplicates and caller order are not erased; an index table deliberately maps duplicates to their last slot, matching the Python dictionary comprehension. Backend results are consumed with Rust `zip`, reproducing silent truncation instead of inventing a length error. Reset logger callbacks receive the entire raw optional-observation batch because that is the current Python behavior, even though a per-worker value might appear more intuitive. Reset invalidity retires workers, while step invalidity only yields a placeholder. Defaults are owned clones, matching Python deep-copy isolation for the supported Rust value graph. Typed errors replace Python assertions and component exceptions without changing reached state or callback order.
- Plugin boundary: `FiniteVectorBackend` owns batching and transport and can be implemented by in-process, subprocess, shared-memory, remote, replay, or test backends. `FiniteObservationPredicate` owns observation validity and can use the bundled recursive Qlib predicate or a domain-specific validator. Each `FiniteVectorLogger` independently receives lifecycle, reset, and step callbacks. The coordinator owns ordering, retirement, remapping, defaults, and error-stage attribution; these traits are process-local Rust plugin seams, not a stable binary ABI.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing third-party `indexmap::IndexSet` supplies deterministic alive-worker storage, `tracing` emits the Python-compatible unguarded-reset warning, and `thiserror` supplies typed stage diagnostics. The bundled concrete predicate reuses the previous `ndarray`/`half`-based `FiniteObservation` implementation. A custom ordered set, logging facade, or error hierarchy was intentionally avoided. Async/process crates are deferred until a concrete Subproc/Shmem transport slice requires them.

## Finite dummy vector backend

- Contract: Construct at least one in-process worker by invoking the same supplied environment factory once per worker in ascending worker-id order. For reset and synchronous step, preserve Tianshou 0.4.10's two-phase behavior: send to every requested worker first, then receive in requested order. A repeated worker id therefore executes repeatedly during send but every matching output slot observes the final result retained by that worker. Require exact action/id cardinality before step mutation; report invalid ids only when reached, retaining mutations from earlier sends; and stop at the first factory, reset, or step failure with its worker id.
- In scope: Object-safe process-local environment and environment-factory plugins; eager repeated factory construction; empty-concurrency rejection; deterministic sequential reset/step; requested-id ordering and duplicates; final-result cloning for repeated receive slots; empty batches; exact action-count validation; invalid-id, factory, reset, and step failures with partial-mutation boundaries; erasure through `FiniteVectorBackend`; composition with the migrated `FiniteVectorEnv`; and live AST characterization of Qlib's empty multiple-inheritance class plus factory repetition/selection structure.
- Out of scope: A direct adapter for `EnvironmentResetRunner`; close, seed, render, and Gym attribute delegation; asynchronous `wait_num`/timeout behavior; NumPy stacking/object arrays; `FiniteSubprocVectorEnv`; `FiniteShmemVectorEnv`; the final `vectorize_env` selector; environment-factory serialization; logger implementation details; trainer deep-copy policy; Python bindings; plugin discovery; and a stable binary ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: The Rust backend deliberately separates the send loop from the receive projection instead of using a convenient per-worker map, because Tianshou's `DummyEnvWorker.send` overwrites its retained result and duplicate ids consequently return the final result in every duplicate slot. Action-count mismatch is validated before any worker call, matching synchronous `BaseVectorEnv.step`; id validity is checked only as each send is reached, preserving prior mutations. Rust uses typed errors instead of Python assertion, `IndexError`, and arbitrary worker exceptions. Zero workers return `FiniteDummyBuildError::Empty` rather than reproducing Tianshou's accidental `workers[0]` `IndexError`. A factory may still intentionally return workers sharing interior state, matching Qlib's warning that incorrectly shared factory closures are caller responsibility.
- Plugin boundary: `FiniteEnvironment` is the narrow single-worker reset/step seam. `FiniteEnvironmentFactory` is object-safe and has a blanket implementation for `FnMut`, allowing constructor closures, dependency-injection objects, replay workers, or future process proxies. `FiniteDummyBackend` owns only eager construction and the sequential batch protocol, then implements the existing `FiniteVectorBackend`. These are statically linked Rust seams rather than runtime-discovered plugins.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. Existing `thiserror` supplies build/runtime diagnostics. Sequential `Vec` storage is required by indexed worker semantics and the standard library is sufficient for the short deterministic send/receive loops. `rayon` was rejected because parallel execution would violate Dummy's ordered single-process contract; Tokio, IPC, shared-memory, and serialization crates are deferred to the corresponding Subproc/Shmem slices. General-purpose coordinator ordering and logging continue to reuse `indexmap` and `tracing` in the upstream slice.
