## Reset-runner finite worker adapter

- Contract: Treat each migrated `EnvironmentResetRunner` as one finite environment worker. Reset returns its observation unchanged, including the first invalid observation produced when a finite seed source exhausts. Step clones the borrowed policy action into the owned runner API and maps the resulting observation, scalar reward, done flag, ordered logs, and auxiliary info into populated `FiniteBackendStep` fields. Reset/step failures cross the object-safe worker boundary as `EnvironmentPluginError` while retaining the complete typed source display. A repeated reset after permanent death and a step before reset or after exhaustion remain errors; the first exhaustion observation remains a normal value so `FiniteVectorEnv` can retire that worker.
- In scope: A generic implementation for all compatible `EnvironmentResetRunner` type parameters; reset success; step success and full info ownership; simulator-factory reset failure; repeated-dead reset; step-before-reset; exhausted step; composition with `FiniteDummyBackend`; one shared factory constructing two independent seeded runners; independent worker state/action histories; different actions in the same batch; invalid-observation retirement; final vector zombie transition; and composed use of the existing live `EnvWrapper.reset`, `EnvWrapper.step`, finite-observation, Dummy, and vector-coordinator characterizations.
- Out of scope: Cloning arbitrary trainer-owned interpreter/reward templates—the factory remains responsible for producing independent runner instances; close/seed/render/space delegation; NumPy batch stacking; subprocess/shared-memory execution; cross-process serialization; `vectorize_env`; Python bindings; runtime plugin discovery; and a stable binary ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: The adapter is a blanket Rust trait implementation rather than a wrapper allocation, so the existing runner remains the single owner of episode state and log history. `EnvironmentResetRunner` already converts Python `StopIteration` during the first exhausted reset into its invalid observation; the adapter deliberately does not reinterpret that value as an error. At the object-safe plugin boundary, typed Rust reset/step enums are converted to their stable display text because `FiniteEnvironment` has one transport-neutral error domain. Every successful step field is owned and wrapped in `Some`; this matches a concrete `EnvWrapper.step`, which always supplies observation, float reward, done, and info.
- Plugin boundary: `EnvironmentResetRunner` now directly implements `FiniteEnvironment<Observation, PolicyAction, f64, EnvironmentStepInfo<...>>`. Any Dummy factory can therefore return boxed migrated runners without a project-specific wrapper. Simulator, state/action interpreter, reward, auxiliary-info, logger, seed source, observation space, worker factory, backend, observation predicate, and vector logger remain independently replaceable at their existing seams.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. The adapter reuses existing `EnvironmentStepInfo`, `FiniteBackendStep`, and `EnvironmentPluginError` DTOs and error infrastructure. A mapping crate or dynamic dispatch helper would only duplicate two explicit compatibility conversions. Independent worker ownership is supplied by repeated factory construction; `Arc`/`Mutex` remains confined to existing logs and test observability rather than being introduced into runner state.

## Finite subprocess wire protocol

- Contract: Preserve the command vocabulary used by Tianshou 0.4.10's `SubprocEnvWorker`: reset, step, close, render, seed, get attribute, and set attribute. Reset, step, close, render, seed, and get-attribute commands require matching replies; successful set-attribute is deliberately one-way. Qlib's `FiniteSubprocVectorEnv` and `FiniteShmemVectorEnv` remain marker subclasses over the corresponding Tianshou vector environments. Unknown commands remain protocol errors. The Rust protocol adds an explicit version, request ID, typed reply kind, and structured environment/protocol/panic failures so a parent does not have to infer every remote error from EOF.
- In scope: Generic owned action, observation, reward, info, and auxiliary payload DTOs; stable command/reply discriminants; optional shared-memory reset observation; optional missing attributes; one-way set-attribute semantics; structured failures; version and request-ID validation; expected-reply validation; deterministic fixed-width little-endian Bincode; rejection of empty, oversized, malformed, and trailing-byte frames; configurable frame size with a 16 MiB default; and live Qlib AST plus frozen Tianshou 0.4.10 dispatch characterization.
- Out of scope: Starting or supervising child processes; stdin/stdout transport; asynchronous request scheduling; timeout, cancellation, EOF, panic capture, kill, wait, and cleanup policy; environment factory transfer; shared-memory allocation and observation reconstruction; NumPy object-array compatibility; `vectorize_env`; trainer integration; Python bindings; runtime plugin discovery; and a stable external ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: `SetAttribute` exposes `expected_reply() == None`, matching the upstream child loop's lack of `pipe.send`. A failure response is accepted for every command, including a failed one-way mutation. Reset carries `Option<Observation>` so the later shared-memory worker can acknowledge a reset without duplicating the observation in the pipe. `GetAttribute` returns `Option<Payload>` to preserve upstream missing-attribute `None`. Seed accepts an optional payload and its result is optional so the later worker can preserve both legacy `env.seed` and `env.reset(seed=...)` fallback behavior. Successful replies are checked against both request ID and command kind before use.
- Plugin boundary: The wire module is runtime-independent and generic over all application DTOs. A future subprocess backend can own transport and lifecycle while reusing this codec, and a shared-memory backend can reuse the same control plane while replacing only observation storage. The existing `FiniteVectorBackend` remains the batching plugin seam. Cross-process payload implementations must be explicitly owned, Serde/Bincode-compatible DTOs; formats based on `deserialize_any`, including `serde_json::Value`, are not valid Bincode wire payloads.
- Dependencies: No dependency was added. The implementation deliberately reuses the existing mature `serde`, `bincode` 1.3, and `thiserror` crates. Serde owns the DTO contract, Bincode owns compact deterministic serialization, and thiserror owns typed diagnostics. The next runtime slice should use Tokio's maintained async process API with piped stdin/stdout and `kill_on_drop`, plus `tokio-util::codec::LengthDelimitedCodec` with its maximum-frame setting; that keeps process supervision and length framing out of bespoke code.

## Finite subprocess Tokio runtime

- Contract: Preserve Tianshou 0.4.10's sequential pipe exchange for one subprocess worker: write one length-delimited request, receive the correlated reply when the command requires one, and leave successful set-attribute one-way. A cooperative close may end the worker normally; EOF, truncated or oversized frames, malformed payloads, wrong request IDs, I/O failures, and bounded-operation timeouts are typed parent-side failures. Every timed-out or explicitly terminated child is killed and reaped, and dropping a live transport requests process termination.
- In scope: Tokio child startup with piped stdin/stdout and `kill_on_drop`; program arguments and working directory; `LengthDelimitedCodec` framing with the protocol frame limit; bounded write, read, input-close, wait, kill, and reap operations; typed exit status; request/reply correlation through the completed protocol; sequential worker dispatch over arbitrary Tokio streams; all seven commands; one-way set-attribute; structured environment and protocol failures; panic capture for string, owned-string, and opaque payloads; handler-reply validation; real Windows/Python subprocess characterization; and deterministic in-memory duplex tests.
- Out of scope: `FiniteSubprocessBackend` worker pooling and batched send-all/receive-all ordering; environment-factory serialization or a registered worker executable; concurrent requests on one child; trainer construction; shared-memory allocation/reconstruction; NumPy object-array compatibility; the final `vectorize_env` selector; Python bindings; runtime plugin discovery; and a stable external ABI.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust adds explicit frame limits, operation timeouts, structured failures, request IDs, panic conversion, and orphan prevention where upstream can block indefinitely or surface only EOF. A failed set-attribute cannot be returned on the same one-way call; the worker emits a failure and exits, so a later parent read observes that pending response or correlation failure. `tokio::process::Child::kill` is followed by the shared wait path so cleanup always returns the project-owned `FiniteSubprocessExitStatus`. The worker remains sequential because one pipe pair represents one environment and upstream ordering is observable.
- Plugin boundary: `FiniteSubprocessCommandHandler` is a `Send`, object-safe command plugin with a closure adapter; type erasure deliberately gives every handler one worker state machine and permits environment, replay, proxy, or test implementations. `FiniteSubprocessLifecycle` is an object-safe kill/wait seam used by Tokio children and deterministic cleanup tests. `FiniteSubprocessExitStatus` keeps platform-specific `std::process::ExitStatus` out of that boundary. These are statically linked Rust extension seams, not dynamically discovered binary plugins.
- Dependencies: Added `tokio` 1.53.1 with only `io-util`, `macros`, `process`, `rt`, and `time`; `tokio-util` 0.7.19 with only `codec`; `futures-util` 0.3.34 with `sink` and `std`; and `bytes` 1.12.1. Tokio and tokio-util are MIT and require Rust 1.71; futures-util is MIT/Apache-2.0 and requires Rust 1.71; bytes is MIT and requires Rust 1.57. Tokio owns maintained cross-platform process supervision, tokio-util owns bounded length framing, futures-util supplies the standard sink/stream extensions, and bytes supplies codec frames. No bespoke async runtime, framing parser, or process abstraction was introduced.

## Finite subprocess batched backend

- Contract: Preserve Tianshou 0.4.10 synchronous vector semantics used by Qlib's marker subclass: validate the selected environment ids and exact action cardinality before mutation, send every request before receiving replies, receive in selected-id order, and treat duplicate ids as separate sequential exchanges. A healthy close performs the full close/reply/input-close/wait lifecycle one worker at a time in environment order. Any incomplete batch, malformed or mismatched reply, remote failure, or lifecycle failure poisons the pool; cleanup then force-terminates every worker and retains the first cleanup error.
- In scope: One subprocess worker per finite environment; wrapping `u64` request ids; reset and step batching; duplicate ids; typed remote, send, receive, correlation, unexpected-reply, close-input, wait, and terminate failures; open/poisoned/closed states; sequential healthy close; all-worker forced cleanup; `FiniteVectorBackend` integration; injectable worker and runtime factories; program-list validation; and real Tokio/Python worker execution.
- Rust technology: The backend uses object-safe Rust traits for transport and factory plugins, Tokio's maintained current-thread runtime for synchronous orchestration, Serde-owned generic DTO bounds, and the existing bounded Bincode protocol. The production program factory and `FiniteSubprocessTransport` adapter live with the transport module; Qlib-specific batch ordering, request correlation, and poison-state policy remain local code because no third-party crate supplies those semantics.
- Plugin boundary: `FiniteSubprocessWorker` exposes only bounded byte frames and lifecycle futures, so alternative process, remote, replay, and shared-memory control transports do not leak concrete Tokio I/O types into the coordinator. `FiniteSubprocessWorkerFactory` owns per-environment construction, and `FiniteSubprocessRuntimeFactory` owns executor creation. `FiniteSubprocessProgramFactory` is the bundled Tokio process implementation. These are process-local Rust plugin seams, not a stable binary ABI; the versioned wire protocol is the cross-process compatibility boundary.

## Finite shared-memory observation transport

- Contract: Freeze Tianshou 0.4.10's split transport: reset and step observations use one fixed worker-local shared buffer, while command/reply ordering and lifecycle remain on the subprocess pipe. The producer completes the observation write before sending the control reply; the consumer receives and validates that reply before reading the mapping. Reset and step control replies must not carry an inline observation. Other reply kinds stay entirely on the control plane.
- In scope: Cross-platform file-backed memory mapping; fixed capacity; versioned 32-byte header; request-id correlation; payload length and CRC32 validation; non-overwriting creation; exact-size opening; owned observation copies; reset/step rehydration; passthrough close/render/seed/attribute/failure replies; all subprocess send/receive/close/wait/terminate delegation; typed uninitialized, corrupt, unsupported-version, oversize, stale-id, decode, inline-observation, EOF, and re-encode failures; per-environment owner directories and mappings; child path/capacity environment injection; partial-construction rollback; production backend construction; real child writer handshake; cleanup after close/drop; and registry selection under `shmem`.
- Compatibility decision: Tianshou stores recursive NumPy leaves directly in `multiprocessing.Array`; the Rust transport stores an owned Bincode observation payload in the mapped data plane. The public `FiniteVectorBackend` already returns owned observations and subsequently batches them, so this preserves observable values and the pipe/shared-memory split without exposing aliasing views. Request ids remove the upstream stale-buffer race. CRC32 detects accidental corruption; it is integrity checking, not authentication.
- Rust technology and safety: `memmap2` 0.9.11 supplies maintained Windows/Unix mappings and `crc32fast` 1.5 supplies the checksum. `memmap2` requires an unsafe mapping call because external mutation cannot be proven by Rust's borrow checker. That single call is isolated in the dedicated `qlib-shmem` crate behind a safe copy-in/copy-out API and a documented control-channel synchronization contract. `qlib-core` retains its workspace-wide `unsafe_code = "forbid"` policy.
- Plugin boundary: `FiniteShmemWorker` implements the existing object-safe `FiniteSubprocessWorker`, so the proven batched backend, Tokio runtime, poison policy, close ordering, and `FiniteVectorBackend` integration are reused unchanged. `FiniteShmemBackendPlugin` resolves named child programs through the existing program-resolver seam and is registered under the stable `shmem` selector. The mapped-region implementation is a replaceable data-plane crate; the versioned subprocess DTO remains the cross-process control boundary. The child writer can be Rust, Python, or another process as long as it implements the documented mapped frame and control ordering.
- Evidence: Official Tianshou v0.4.10 source fixes the supported numeric leaf types, recursive Dict/Tuple layout, construction-before-spawn behavior, child write-before-reply order, parent reply-before-read order, and passthrough lifecycle commands. Registry tests cover resolver replacement/failure, shared-memory build failure, and real registered process selection.

## RL producer/consumer data queue

- Contract: Preserve Qlib's ephemeral single-activation queue; automatic nonzero capacity when `queue_maxsize == 0`; finite repeat, `-1` infinite repeat, shuffled or sequential epoch sampling; bounded producer backpressure; public item insertion; first/subsequent consumer wait behavior; ordered results even when dataset reads run concurrently; producer completion; early cleanup; exhaustion; and cleanup-on-drop. Dataset, sampler, out-of-range, consumer-disconnect, and panic failures are surfaced as typed diagnostics instead of being lost in a Python daemon-thread traceback.
- In scope: `DataQueueConfig`; automatic capacity; object-safe `DataQueueDataset` and `DataQueueSampler`; bundled sequential and random samplers; zero-worker sequential loading; ordered multi-worker prefetch; bounded output; completion notification; finite, zero, negative, and infinite repeats; activation/consumer guards; producer error retention; dataset and sampler failures; invalid sample indices; sequential and parallel panic capture; cancellation while blocked or loading; idempotent cleanup; manual `put`; iterator termination; and live AST characterization of Qlib defaults, methods, timeouts, daemon production, `10**18` infinite sentinel, and PyTorch loader arguments.
- Compatibility decisions: Rust uses a real unbounded epoch counter for `repeat == -1` rather than Python's finite `10**18` approximation. A negative repeat other than `-1` remains empty. Unlike Python's daemon thread, every Rust producer is joined during cleanup/drop, so no producer or worker is orphaned. The public consumer yields a producer error once and then terminates; normal completion terminates without an error item. Multi-worker reads may finish out of order but are resequenced before entering the output channel, matching PyTorch DataLoader's default ordered delivery.
- Dependencies: `crossbeam-channel` 0.5.16 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, MSRV 1.60) provides maintained bounded MPMC channels, timeout sends, completion notification, and backpressure. `rand` 0.9.2 provides maintained in-place slice shuffling while sharing the existing `getrandom` 0.3 dependency used by Arrow's `ahash`; it supports the workspace Rust 1.85 baseline. `std::thread::scope`, atomics, and join handles own lifecycle and borrowing. The remaining local code is Qlib-specific epoch scheduling, ordered resequencing, and error attribution.
- Plugin boundary: `DataQueueDataset<T>` isolates sequence length/index loading and can wrap in-memory, Arrow, storage, or remote datasets. `DataQueueSampler` owns each epoch's indices and supports deterministic, distributed, weighted, or externally seeded sampling. Both are process-local object-safe seams; channel transport is deliberately private so a future OS-process adapter can replace it without changing trainer-facing lifecycle.
- Differential evidence: The Python fixture parses the live `D:\code\github\qlib\qlib\rl\utils\data_queue.py` and verifies constructor defaults `[1, true, 0, 0]`, 5.0/0.5-second consumer timeouts, daemon activation, the `10**18` infinite-repeat sentinel, public method surface, and DataLoader's item-wise configuration. Rust tests verify the corresponding observable lifecycle plus deterministic ordering and structured failure behavior.

## Training vessel initial-state queues

- Status: `done` for this slice only; whole-Qlib migration remains active.

## Training vessel metric logging

- Status: `done` for the stated numeric/scalar logging slice; the full migration goal remains active.
- Source: `qlib/rl/trainer/vessel.py::TrainingVesselBase.{log,log_dict}`, called by default `TrainingVessel.train/validate/test` after collector and policy results are merged.
- Contract: Reduce ndarray/list numeric values over all elements before looking up the trainer; then read the current iteration, add one using arbitrary-sized integers, format the metric, and emit `[Iter N] name = value`. Non-array custom formatting happens after trainer access. `log_dict` preserves insertion order and stops on the first failure without rolling back earlier messages; an empty map does not require a trainer. The current iteration is read separately for every message.
- In scope: Flat Arrow representations of numeric ndarray/rectangular-list inputs, every Boolean/integer width and Float16/32/64, dtype-aware accumulation and final rounding, empty/NaN/infinite values, source-compatible scalar formatting, arbitrary-sized integer scalars, booleans/null/text, delayed custom formatting, ordered maps and duplicate replacement, default tracing delivery, reducer/formatter/sink failures, and live weak trainer binding.
- Dependencies: No new crate. Existing Arrow cast and sum kernels provide numerical conversion/reduction; Boolean/integer/Float64 accumulate in Float64 while Float16/32 accumulate in Float32. `half` rounds Float16 results and `num-bigint` preserves Python integer ranges. `indexmap` supplies stable dictionary behavior, `tracing` supplies delivery, and `thiserror` supplies typed errors. Standard Rust shortest float formatting supplies digits, with a small Qlib/Python compatibility adapter for lowercase NaN and explicit, two-digit-minimum signed exponents. The older account-only float formatter is not reused because its fixed formatting does not handle this broader scientific-notation contract.
- Official references: [NumPy mean](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.mean.html) documents integer Float64 accumulation and Float16 Float32 intermediates. The installed NumPy `_core._methods._mean` and Arrow 59.2.0 `aggregate::sum` source were inspected for dtype and empty-reduction behavior. Existing Arrow general-purpose kernels are reused instead of implementing a new mean engine.
- Plugin boundaries: `TrainingMetricReducer` can supply alternate reduction/type behavior, `TrainingMetricDisplay` defers opaque-value formatting until after iteration lookup, and `TrainingMetricSink` controls delivery and failures. `TrainingMetricValue::Numeric` accepts a dtype-preserving Arrow array; bindings/collectors must flatten rectangular lists/ndarrays before this boundary. No dataframe or ML-specific type leaks into the logging service.
- Numerical contract: Exact message comparisons cover ordinary small arrays, every dtype, fractional Float16/32, NaN/infinities, lists, scalars, and scientific notation. A 1,000-element finite positive dataset compares Arrow/NumPy means with a stated forward-error bound (`n * epsilon * max_input` for Float32/64 and one final half-precision rounding step for Float16). Arrow and NumPy may use different summation orders; last-bit equality and consequently byte-identical long-reduction output are not claimed. Cancellation-heavy numeric equivalence beyond that bound is not established by this test.

They additionally compare 262 IEEE-bit-pattern float representations, explicit fixed/scientific boundary texts, null/unsupported dtype rejection, Float32 overflow, Float16 maximum finite mean, all empty floating dtypes, disabled/enabled tracing delivery, negative iterations, duplicate key order, custom reducer success/failure, custom formatter success/failure, sink failure before the second metric, expired/unassigned/inaccessible trainer errors, and empty maps.

## Default training vessel collection/update orchestration

- Status: `done` for the collection/update orchestration slice. The full Qlib migration goal remains active.
- Source: `qlib/rl/trainer/vessel.py::TrainingVessel.{train,validate,test}` together with the actual `FiniteVectorEnv.collector_guard` context manager. Trainer `fit`/`test` callers create phase environments and invoke these methods; concrete collector/replay-buffer/ML runtimes are dependencies, not implemented by an interface declaration.
- Contract: Switch policy mode outside the guard. Train constructs a buffer using capacity and environment count, then a collector with exploration enabled; read live `fast_dev_run` once when absent and twice when present; collect the selected episode count; obtain the collector's buffer before validating duplicate update keywords; call update with sample size zero and that same mutable buffer; merge update metrics over collection metrics without reordering existing keys; log the merged metrics before done hooks. Validation/test construct a collector with no supplied buffer and default disabled exploration, then collect `INF * environment_count` steps, log, and never update the policy.
- Exhaustion/lifecycle: Body exhaustion returns `Ok(None)` after done hooks, including exhaustion from collector construction or policy update, rather than fabricating metrics. Ordinary body errors clear the guard and skip done hooks. Ready-hook failure leaves the guarded flag set, matching the source's placement outside its try/finally. Mode-switch errors propagate outside the guard, including exhaustion. No Rust panic-unwind compatibility is claimed.
- Dependencies: No new crate. Existing `indexmap` provides ordered keyword/metric maps and overwrite-without-reordering semantics; `num-bigint` computes the finite integer evaluation budget without machine-word overflow; `thiserror` generates typed errors. Existing Arrow/logging and finite-vector services are composed unchanged except for a generic typed-error collector guard. Local code is limited to source-specific ordering and delegation, not a replacement ML or replay-buffer engine.
- Plugin boundaries: `TrainingRunPolicy` owns mode switching and policy updates; `TrainingCollectorFactory` constructs buffers and collectors; `TrainingRunCollector` owns collection and buffer access. Policy/environment are reborrowed per operation, never retained as aliased mutable references. The collector may retain shared handles and owns its buffer. `None` from collector buffer access is forwarded to the policy, not rejected by an invented vessel validation. These are linked Rust interfaces, not a dynamic-library ABI.

## RL log writer lifecycle and metric buffer

- Status: `done` for the writer lifecycle and numeric buffer slice. The complete Qlib migration remains unfinished and the goal remains active.
- Source/callers: `qlib/rl/utils/log.py::{LogWriter,LogBuffer}`. Finite vector environments call reset/step/ready/done methods. `Trainer._metrics_callback` reads global episodes and latest/collect metrics. Console/CSV writers subclass the same lifecycle and remain separate output sinks.
- Contract: Steps increment global/collect counters and activate the environment before checking reset state. Length/reward/history mutation precedes the step hook; completion counters precede the episode hook. Missing state, missing log, and hook failures retain the exact preceding changes. Done steps do not auto-reset their histories, so repeated done calls before reset reuse the growing episode history. Reset replaces only that environment's length/rewards/logs. Clear/ready reset collect counters and active ids but retain global counters and all environment histories.
- Aggregation: Only values identified as Python floats participate in numeric buffering; integers, booleans, strings, tensors, and other objects are ignored. Float-only general aggregation uses a sum for the exact name `reward`, a mean otherwise; mixed-type general aggregation returns the first value, and empty aggregation fails. Each completed episode overwrites latest metrics and adds to the ordered aggregate sums. Collect means divide by all completed episodes, including episodes that omitted a particular metric. Empty completed episodes still produce an empty latest map and invoke the callback. No completed episode leaves latest metrics unavailable. Finalization invokes the collect callback even with no episodes.
- Dependencies: Existing Arrow Float64 sum kernels provide numeric reduction; existing IndexMap supplies stable grouping, overwrite order, histories, and active-id sets; Serde supplies typed checkpoint encoding; BigInt supplies unbounded counters; Thiserror supplies diagnostics. Only the existing IndexMap serde feature was enabled. Cargo initially selected 2.14.1 while resolving the feature edit; the manifest now pins `=2.14.0` to retain the previously used implementation, whose local feature declaration was inspected. No new crate was introduced. Local code implements Qlib's counter/update/filter/grouping/callback rules, not a general logging or reduction library.
- Plugin/representation boundaries: `RlLogWriterHooks` supports replaceable step, episode, clear, and finalization sinks. `RlLogBuffer` supplies concrete numeric aggregation hooks and a fallible callback receiving immutable writer/buffer views. `RlLogValue<V>` explicitly distinguishes Python-float values from adapter-owned nonnumeric values; an upstream adapter must retain that distinction (`np.float32` versus `np.float64` is tested). Use shared handles inside `V` when object identity matters. Arbitrary integral log levels are supported. These are linked Rust interfaces, not a stable native ABI.
- Checkpoints: Writer state and buffer state are separately exposed typed views and restored as owned DTOs, with buffer restoration preceding writer restoration. Serde round trips preserve counters, histories, key ordering, and optional latest-metric state; missing `latest_metrics` is rejected even though its value may be null. The API does not emulate Python's arbitrary mutable dictionary aliases, malformed untyped checkpoint partial assignments, pickle, or Torch files. Bincode requires a compatible caller-selected opaque value type; native String payloads are tested, and JSON-oriented opaque values remain suitable for JSON.
- Finite environment integration: Both writer and buffer implement the actual `FiniteVectorLogger` interface for typed `RlLogInfo` payloads. Tests run a real `FiniteDummyBackend` through two complete episodes and final dataset exhaustion, confirming two episode callbacks, one collect callback, correct means, and zero unguarded-reset warnings. Missing reward is an adapter representation error before lifecycle mutation; absent info/log is reported after the source-compatible counter/reward mutations. The existing `EnvironmentStepInfo`/Python object decoding layer still needs a value-classifying bridge.
- Tests: Five focused tests execute the live Qlib classes via AST with real NumPy and compare seven lifecycle scenarios, three buffer scenarios, ten aggregation scenarios, and three restored-count division cases. ## Trainer runtime state and metric callback bridge

- Status: `done`; five Trainer-focused tests, the deterministic queue-cleanup regression, strict Clippy, full workspace tests, stable/nightly instrumented suites, and both exact-count coverage gates pass.
- Source: `qlib/rl/trainer/trainer.py::{Trainer.initialize,initialize_iter,_metrics_callback,_min_loglevel}` and constructor-established runtime metadata. The fixture executes the real constructor with lightweight logger classes to establish which attributes exist before initialization; full configured construction is not claimed by this slice.
- Contract: Construction sets the stage to `train` but leaves iteration, episode, stop flag, and metrics uninitialized. `initialize` resets stop/iteration/episode/stage but preserves existing metrics; `initialize_iter` replaces only the metric map. Episode notifications take precedence when both flags are true, update the current episode before reading episode metrics, and preserve that update after read failures. Collect notifications do not update the episode counter. Only the exact stage `val` prefixes every incoming key with `val/`, including already-prefixed names; other stage strings pass keys unchanged. Ordered updates preserve old-key positions, retain absent keys, and append new keys in provider order.
- Error ordering: Missing provider state/read errors occur before destination-map access. If neither event is selected, validation attempts prefixing first and reports missing event even with an uninitialized metric map; non-validation stages resolve the destination first, matching Python's AttributeError versus UnboundLocalError ordering. Empty incoming maps still require an initialized target. Errors are typed Rust equivalents, not byte-identical Python exception strings.
- Dependencies: No new dependency or feature change. Existing IndexMap owns ordered updates, Serde derives typed runtime metadata serialization, BigInt retains unbounded iteration/episode counters, and Thiserror derives errors. Standard Arc/Mutex provide shared ownership and synchronized access; iterator minimum implements the small live-level query. LogBuffer remains the sole numeric aggregation engine; no duplicate reducer or logger was written.
- Plugin boundary: `RlTrainerMetricSource<M>` provides fallible global-episode, episode-metric, and collect-metric reads. Metric values are moved without Clone or serialization requirements. `RlLogBufferMetricSource` is the concrete adapter to the completed log buffer and converts numeric values with `From<f64>` when a custom metric type is selected. `RlTrainerRuntime` implements the existing `TrainingTrainerView`, so vessel bindings read live iteration and development settings from the same state updated by buffer callbacks.
- Ownership and failures: Runtime read/update closures execute under one mutex and must not reenter it. A panic during mutation poisons subsequent reads, writes, config updates, vessel access, and buffer callback delivery; it is not silently recovered. The buffer callback retains an Arc to runtime metadata, matching Python bound-method retention. Runtime metadata owns no callbacks/loggers, so this is acyclic. Vessel bindings remain weak. The source liveness test verifies that retained callbacks still update state after the direct owner reference is dropped, and state is released when the callback is released (after explicit GC in Python).
- Evidence: Five tests cover 27 source-executed metric scenarios, constructor/initialize/iteration snapshots, five minimum-level examples, callback liveness, all provider errors, missing initialization, both/zero event flags, train/val/test/custom stages, exact key order, double prefixes, sparse metric replacement, serialization, non-Clone opaque values, NaN/infinity preservation, 10^30 iterations, development-setting changes, and poisoning. Integration uses the actual RlLogBuffer to drive three episodes across train/val stages, then the actual TrainingVesselBinding and TrainingVesselLog to emit an iteration-correct message from the shared runtime.

Cleanup now exposes a private join boundary while retaining cancel/drain/join/drain ordering. A release-channel regression asserts that the first buffered value is drained, a late value exists when join returns, and cleanup removes it before reporting exhaustion. This deterministically exercises the real second drain without sleeps, coverage exclusions, or test-specific production behavior.

Log levels and development counts retain existing i64 boundaries; generic counters remain unbounded.

## Trainer fit/test lifecycle driver

- Status: `done`; five focused tests, strict Clippy, full workspace tests, stable/nightly instrumented suites, and both exact-count coverage gates pass.

A suppressed execution failure retains the environment until a replacement has been constructed or fit/test returns. Entry failure skips exit; environment construction failure still calls exit; exit can suppress or replace the original error. ## Trainer named checkpoint graph

- Status: `done`; six focused tests, formatting, strict Clippy, full workspace tests, stable/nightly instrumented suites, and exact per-file/total coverage gates pass. This completes the graph traversal slice, not the full Qlib migration.
- Contract: Name components from lowercase source type names with per-type occurrence suffixes; retain collision overwrite and insertion order. Save vessel, then named callbacks, then named loggers, then runtime metadata. Restore in the same graph order followed by sequential metadata assignment; missing later fields and plugin failures preserve earlier side effects. Empty registries do not read their checkpoint map. Extra checkpoint entries are ignored.
- Design: Reuse IndexMap, Serde, BigInt, and Thiserror. Separate typed checkpoint payloads from codecs; represent missing fields distinctly from present null/optional values. Keep component payloads generic so tensor/runtime adapters are not forced into JSON. Use an explicit restore adapter with the existing Trainer driver.
- Evidence: 33 live-source graph scenarios compare save/load call order, complete output, partial runtime state, and all component-side effects. They cover collisions that omit overwritten objects, every component save/load failure, every missing graph/metadata field, uninitialized runtime fields, empty registries with absent maps, and ignored extra entries. Seven naming matrices cover empty/repeated names, mixed case, real-name/suffix collisions, Greek final sigma, dotted I, and German sharp S. Other tests cover distinct missing versus present-null fields, malformed typed values, complete JSON/Bincode round trips, generic non-Clone/non-Serialize/non-Default component payloads, shared metric payload identity, poisoned runtime failure after graph side effects, and concrete adapter errors.
- Integration: Borrowed checkpoint component handles reference the same live state consumed by a real RlTrainerDriver callback and RlLogBuffer. TrainingVesselState delegates real policy state through the existing envelope. After state corruption, RlTrainerCheckpointRestore restores vessel weights, callback counter, complete writer/buffer state, and Trainer metadata before on_fit_start; the next iteration resumes from 12 to 13 and updates the restored policy/callback values. A subsequent missing-vessel restore fails after attachment and before fit-start. RlLogWriter's base state and RlLogBuffer's complete state have separate explicit payload types.
- Ownership/representation: Component payloads are moved on save and borrowed on load without cloning/coercion. The registry borrows live components and computes names before each group traversal; it does not instantiate copies. Runtime metadata/metric maps are owned snapshots and require M:Clone; shared handles inside M preserve opaque value identity, but arbitrary Python dictionary aliases are not emulated. Metadata assignment uses one lock after plugin traversal, preserving source sequential partial assignments without a check/update race. No lock is held across plugin calls.
- Serialization: RlCheckpointField separates absence from a present optional/null payload and uses existing Serde for present values. Missing JSON fields remain absent until load traversal reaches them; type decoding still belongs to the typed frontend. Positional Bincode encoding is tested for complete documents only; partial documents require a map-oriented format. The buffer payload is an explicit writer/buffer DTO rather than the flat Python dictionary. BigInt encoding follows its existing Serde representation. No byte-compatible Torch, pickle, or Python arbitrary-object encoding is claimed.

## EarlyStopping callback

- Status: `done`; seven focused tests, 74 live-source cases, formatting, strict Clippy, complete workspace tests and final stable/nightly exact coverage gates pass. The full Qlib migration goal remains active.

## MetricsWriter callback

- Status: `done`; six focused tests, 138 live-source scenarios, formatting, strict Clippy, full workspace tests and final stable/nightly exact coverage gates pass. Whole-Qlib migration remains active and incomplete.

- Implementation: `crates/qlib-core/src/rl_metrics_writer.rs` implements generic histories, whole-table sink plugins, a concrete CSV/filesystem sink, scalar-column inference and streaming CSV output. The default sink accepts f64, optional f64 and TrainingMetricScalar (including deferred custom displays); an alternate sink can consume other model-owned M directly. Buffering/escaping is delegated to csv. The constructor leaves existing output files intact; a phase hook overwrites only its selected file. No runtime lock is held during sink callbacks.
- Characterization/evidence: The fixture executes actual Callback/MetricsWriter AST methods with installed pandas 2.3.3 and real temporary files. It compares bytes after every event, including mixed train/validation names, val/ case sensitivity, sparse ordered column unions, all-empty rows, quoted/non-ASCII/newline fields, nonfinite/exponent/negative-zero floats, 121 pairwise scalar combinations, custom formatting, constructor/write failures and missing metrics. Integer overflow leaves the previous CSV intact because inference precedes open/truncate; custom formatting occurs after open and preserves actual partial write effects. Real Trainer integration runs fit twice without clearing histories and test without writes. Custom whole-table plugins receive shared non-Serde handles, preserve append-on-failure and can re-enter the Trainer runtime; poisoning/missing-metrics tests prove no append or file write occurs before successful metric access. Generic writers cover header/row write errors and final flush errors, including explicit LF/CRLF.
- Compatibility correction: The first scalar matrix found order-dependent pandas inference: an explicit None before an out-of-range integer bypasses integer-range checks, whereas a missing key/NaN does not. The scanner now preserves that distinction and object short-circuit order, and detects Float64 conversion overflow before opening files. The official [pandas 2.3.3 scalar inference implementation](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/v2.3.3/pandas/_libs/lib.pyx#L2424) was checked against the installed package. Five additional scenarios freeze overflow and ordering. This is a small compatibility adapter over scalar records, not a general replacement dataframe engine; adding Polars would not itself reproduce these pandas-specific rules.

### Checkpoint large-precision continuation (2026-09-03)

- Source contract: Python formats floating `e/E/f/F/g/G/%`, omitted type and C-locale `n` beyond precision 9,999. The [CPython formatter](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Python/formatter_unicode.c) rejects float precision above INT_MAX before conversion; width and precision parsing also detects Py_ssize_t overflow. The prior 81-case candidate matrix established that neither library alone satisfies this surface. Both libraries keep parsed formatting fields private.
- Implementation: `rl_checkpoint_format::floating_engine` recognizes the ASCII large-precision shape with existing Regex. It delegates rounding, exponent selection, sign, negative-zero normalization, grouping and padding to existing pyformat at precision 1,100. Every finite binary64 terminates within 1,074 fractional places, with fewer than 1,100 significant digits; raising precision past 9,999 cannot change its rounded digits or g/omitted-type exponent choice. Nonfinite values and trimmed general/omitted-type forms therefore use the bounded result unchanged. Other forms add only the required zero tail, reducing the delegated width by that tail and inserting before exponent, percent and trailing padding. Integer floating presentations reuse the same path after validation and finite conversion. No new library, floating conversion algorithm or arbitrary fallback to RustPython was introduced.
- Compatibility exception: The local code supplies bounded precision/tail orchestration only because pyformat rejects precision above 9,999 and RustPython has measured z/omitted-type incompatibilities. All numeric representation, grouping and padding remain in the dependency; Regex captures the necessary private metadata. A canonical internal renderer accepts only supported captured flags/types, range-checked widths and precision 1,100; its infallibility is a pinned-library invariant, distinct from fallible user format input. Remove this layer if a maintained engine supplies equivalent unrestricted precision. This does not resolve Python 3.14 fractional grouping.
- Safety: Installed pyformat source uses unchecked width/precision digit accumulation. The public scalar entry now range-checks decimal runs against isize before invoking either dependency, including malformed specs, preventing overflow panics. Captured numeric fields can then be parsed as a checked invariant. Float precision above INT_MAX returns a format error; no impractically large allocation is needed to test that boundary. Integer-to-float overflow remains an error, never infinity coercion.

### Checkpoint fractional grouping continuation (2026-09-03)

- Contract: Python 3.14 permits `,` or `_` after the precision, grouping fractional digits from left to right in threes. Integer and fractional separators are independent. Precision may be omitted (`._`/`.,`); string formatting ignores the fractional separator, integer presentations without precision keep their normal behavior, and `n` rejects it. Nonempty Boolean/None format semantics must survive removal of the new syntax. The [CPython formatter](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Python/formatter_unicode.c) and live oracle establish these rules.
- Reuse and implementation: `rl_checkpoint_format::fractional_scalar` captures the new syntax with existing Regex, delegates numeric conversion, rounding, integer grouping and layout to the pinned engines, and inserts forward-grouped fractional digits only. Added separators reduce delegated width so padding/sign-aware zero grouping retain source behavior. Numeric-body lengths locate the fractional range; searching padded output would confuse literal dot/digit/exponent/percent fills with numeric content. Existing Unicode numeric normalization and large-precision rendering compose with the adapter. No new library, plugin interface, generic parser, numeric conversion algorithm or Unicode table was added. The small local grouping adapter is required because both unadapted dependencies fail 128 of the 198 candidate cases; replace it when a maintained engine supplies equivalent Python 3.14 semantics.

### Native PPO prepared-minibatch loss and real policy updates (2026-09-03)

- Previous goal turn classification: progress (native gradient clipping, fixtures, integration and validation). - Added `rl_candle_ppo::{PpoLossConfig, PpoLossInput, PpoLoss}`. Implements actual discrete prepared-minibatch policy loss, optional dual clipping, value loss with source clipping, entropy regularization and weighted total. Default loss options match Qlib (epsilon 0.3, value clipping/advantage normalization enabled, value coefficient 1, entropy coefficient 0.01, no dual clipping). Returns normalized advantages as well as all loss components and retains the native actor/critic graph. Reuses existing Candle arithmetic/autograd, with no new dependencies, kernels, production Python bridge or Torch-file codec.
- Boundaries are explicit: probabilities [batch, actions], other prepared fields [batch], I64 actions and consistent floating dtype/device. Validates categorical probabilities after renormalization, matching Torch's constructor ordering, then clamps by dtype epsilon before log probabilities. ### Shared raw/parsed calendar eviction and nested loading (2026-09-04)

- Previous goal turn made verification and ledger progress; focused handle 78185 is terminal and its report inspected. This increment changes calendar_provider.rs, its integration tests and unchanged-source fixture to remove the concrete shared-cache dependency identified above. CalendarCache now uses separate parsed-loading and raw-loading mutexes plus a short-lived entries mutex. Lock order is parsed -> raw -> entries; parsed loaders may read raw entries, while neither loader runs under the entries mutex. Callback reentry into parsed loading/clear, or raw callback reentry, remains prohibited. Clear takes both loading locks before removing entries, preventing an in-flight publication from immediately undoing clear.
- Reuses the existing lru crate to maintain one length-bounded/unbounded recency queue for typed raw-URI and parsed-frequency/future keys. Separate typed payload maps avoid downcasts or impossible variant extraction; both maps and recency are updated atomically under one entries lock. Each evicted key removes the corresponding payload. This is not two independent eviction budgets or a custom LRU algorithm. Arc snapshots survive eviction/clear; failed reads do not populate cache. get_or_load_raw takes the exact unnormalized URI and a fallible read callback. Existence checking before every raw lookup and timestamp conversion/resampling after it remain responsibilities of the forthcoming concrete file backend. This change does not implement sys.getsizeof accounting or arbitrary Python cache-key/object mutation.

### Configured native file calendar backend (2026-09-04)

- Previous goal turn made verified production progress.
